CE_notes:
This is one of my favorite concerts of the early Cecil Taylor Unit, so it is part of this year's Cecil Taylor Summer Festival for those of you who haven't had a chance to hear this great performance in excellent sound. It was recorded in 1966 by the S ddeutscher Rundfunk, (which is now part of the S dwestrundfunk) in its recording studio at the Villa Berg in Stuttgart as part of the 'Woche der leichten Musik'. According to the session logs which were acquired from the station's archive by ubu, there were two performances that day. The first of these, the 'Matinekonzert' ('noon concert') has not been broadcast up till now. Apparently it consisted of a piece called Fragments of the Sister Brother Dance (27:30). The afternoon concert was broadcast in 1966 and rebroadcast ca. 1995. This last one was uploaded here in two parts by jason in 2006. Thanks again to all involved. Artwork included. Enjoy!

CE_notes:
Dime user u014945 sent me these files quite some time ago now and asked me to improve the sound where possible.

This is an upgrade to the previously circulating version, but how much of an upgrade...YMMV.

Lineage
The original files seem to be a rip of this CD: https://www.allmusic.com/album/the-complete-birdland-broadcasts-1961-1962-mw0002071178

They came to me as flacs, so: 

flac > cuetools > iZotope RX8 (see note, below) > flac > foobar (splitting back into tracks, tagging)

Note: restoration inclulded a variety of processes. Each session was given a very light auto click removal and then other clicks and pops were cleared up manually
several sessions had hums or buzzes removed on an ad hoc basis (some, where the music seemed to suffer if the fix was applied, did not)

each session was then equalised for slightly 'better' sound smoothing out some of the harshness and opening up the instruments a little - this is noticeable to different degrees depending on the date, as some sounded pretty good already
on some sessions a very gentle hiss reduction was applied

each session was brought to the same loudness.

This link might be helpful (source of much of the original text file): https://mingus.onttonen.info/birdland.html

Taper notes (BARN):
Charlie Hunter is a killer jazz/funk/groove guitarist and bassist (indeed, back then played his own custom 8-string instrument with 5 guitar & 3 bass strings -- though now he has trimmed that down to 7 strings)

his gear allows him to often imitate the sound of a hammond organ with a Leslie cabinet. I first heard of him back in early 1996 from my friend Kevin Landry, and knew that he was somehow signed to Les Claypool's record label. I've since seen him dozens & dozens of times in various combinations (Trio, Quartet, Quintet, in duos with Bobby Previte, in trios with Bobby Previte & DJ Logic, in trios with Bobby Previte & rotating jazz greats, in his band Pound For Pound featuring a vibraphone player, in Garage A Trios with Stanton Moore & Skerik, in TJ Kirk, etc etc.) One of the things about Charlie is that beyond his serious jazz, blues, groove, and funk chops, he's got a great sense of humor in both his playing and his attitude towards his music and performance.

Getting to this recording, BARN225 which I have been trying to get out since as far back as 2012 -- I happened to be in San Francisco on a business trip, and while I was there I met up with my friend Geoff Tischman and we decided to head out to the famous jazz club, the Elbo Room. I'd already had some tapes of some earlier Charlie Hunter shows from the Elbo Room, so I knew he considered it to be kind of his "home venue", so I was psyched to see him! We only made it in time for the late show, and since I wanted to travel lightly, I didn't bring out my whole rig -- just my trusty little Denon DTR-80p, which was tiny (though it chomped through 6 batteries to record a 3 hour show) and easy to toss into my travel bag.

When I got there, I looked to see if anyone else was taping, and there were no other tapers in the house. But I did notice that the band had put one of those Audio Technica 825 stereo mics on stage to tape the show. I asked Charlie if I could get a patch, and he said "Sure!" Well, they must not have been super familiar with the recording gear they were using as I noticed within a minute that the levels were hardly moving -- which indicated that something wasn't set correctly on the recorder, but I knew exactly what it was -- when you patched a microphone into a Tascam DA-P1, you needed to put the "Mic Pad" switch on -20db to avoid analog distortion on the inputs. So as quickly as I could, I fixed this setting and the recording turned out beautiful. So, about the first minute of the recording was somewhat distorted. And if I hadn't been at this show, the band's recording would also have been completely useless (as I'm sure their recording of the early show likely is).

Fast forward to 2012 when I first transferred this show to work on. I worked on it back then...but there was a whole bunch of digital errors in the transfer. So in 2020, I finally got around to attempting another transfer...and most (but not all) of the digital errors in the recording came up as dropouts or little digital "zits" in the same exact places, sadly. Luckily I was able to mask all of the digital errors because they were very very short. After I did my work on this recording, Bill M asked to take a shot at doing his best in trying to correct the analog distortion within the first minute of the recording (my initial take on this was that I was going to edit that part out and fade the recording in once things got properly dialed in) -- and I think his results (while not perfect) do make even the first minute listenable. So, give this a minute into the first track...if you find the opening minute unlistenable, you can just skip past it on your own. Bill also tossed in a little bit of EQ to add some of the deep bass from Charlie's bass strings that the AT-825 can't really capture.

Onto this show -- it's pretty representative of the material he was playing at the time from his first 2 albums...but also contains a STELLAR version of Bob Marley's "Lively Up Yourself" from his track-by-track cover of "Natty Dread" from the "Blue Note Covers Series" albums the label had put out around this time. I actually wish that this recording had a few more of those Marley tracks in the setlist. This was really a high point for this Quintet lineup featuring Charlie's most frequent partner (besides Maybe Bobby Previte) Scott Amendola on drums plus Kenny Brooks (who would go on to play with Bob Weir's band Ratdog) on sax, Calder Spanier on sax, and Chuck McKinnon on trumpet. Alas, this lineup was not able to stay together much longer -- due to the sad fact that Calder was tragically killed at 31 years of age when his stalled car was hit by another driver on his way home from a gig in December of 1997.

After this, the next time I saw Charlie perform was in 1998 with his new band called Pound For Pound which was a radical rethinking of his sound, replacing the horns with a vibraphone.

Enjoy!

Charlie Parker Together With Woody Herman And The 3rd Herd - Mega-rare restored vinyl Bird With The Herd 1951 - Municipal Arena, Kansas City, Missouri 1951-07-22 - speed-corrected and rejoined - A classic, one-time pairing! (mp3 sample included)

During the very early 1970's, the record chain Sam Goody distributed many jazz bootleg releases under their own Alamac label. For this, and for getting someone at a printing plant to make unlicensed extra copies of commercial releases, Steely Dan among them), Sam Goody was busted and nearly closed. The bust didn't help much as they went out of business a couple of years later. (A footnote: someone bought the rights to the name, and did reopen the chain sometime later, but that was a different operation).

Alamac Records product was a plain-white record label with bad printing, with no company name or address on it. The record jackets were plain text on the back, with a single-color front cover (green, brown, etc). The cover could just be text also, or it might have a photo of the artist. The material consisted mostly of privately-made air checks and of radio transcriptions. It's believed the material in this torrent is an air check.

According the the great jazz-research site jazzdisco.org, this is the only release of this material and no known commercial labels have reissued this show. According to Philwoods.com, the record label Alamac is counted as a bootleg. Also, the posting of this torrent has been run by Dime's Moderators in advance.

A historic summit meeting of jazz took place on a scorching summer afternoon in Kansas City when Charlie Parker jined Woody Herman's Third Herd in a series of blazing solos against the background of some of the best Herman repertoire of that period.

Herman's great band serves really as a backdrop for the unique Parker talent and only brief spots by the leader on clarinet, and by Urbie Green on Laura, and Bill Perkins and Dick Hafer on Leo The Lion indicate the many fine talented musicians Herman had in this particular edition of the many Herds he fronted over the years.

Introduction to the Lost and Found Mike the MICrophone Series

Welcome to JEMS Lost and Found Mike the MICrophone series presenting recordings made by legendary taper Mike Millard, AKA Mike the MICrophone, best known for his masters of Led Zeppelin done in and around Los Angeles circa 1975-77. For the complete details on how tapes in this series came to be lost and found again, as well as JEMS' long history with Mike Millard, please refer to the notes in Vol. One: http://www.dimeadozen.org/torrents-details.php?id=500680.

Until 2020, the Lost and Found series presented fresh transfers of previously unavailable first-generation copies made by Mike himself for friends like Stan Gutoski of JEMS, Jim R, Bill C. and Barry G. These sources were upgrades to circulating copies and in most instances marked the only time verified first generation Millard sources had been directly digitized in the torrent era.

That all changed with the discovery of many of Mike Millard s original master tapes.

Yes, you read that correctly, Mike Millard s master cassettes, long rumored to be destroyed or lost, have been found. Not all of them but many, and with them a much more complete picture has emerged of what Millard recorded between his first show in late 1973 and his last in early 1992.

The reason the rediscovery of his master tapes is such a revelation is that we ve been told for decades they were gone. Internet myths suggest Millard destroyed his master tapes before taking his own life, an imprudent detail likely concocted based on the assumption that because his master tapes never surfaced and Mike s mental state was troubled he would do something rash WITH HIS LIFE S WORK. There s also a version of the story where Mike s family dumps the tapes after he dies. Why would they do that?

The truth is Mike s masters remained in his bedroom for many years after his death in 1994. We know at least a few of Millard s friends and acquaintances contacted his mother Lia inquiring about the tapes at the time to no avail. But in the early 2000s, longtime Millard friend Rob S was the one she knew and trusted enough to preserve Mike s work.

The full back story on how Mike s master tapes were saved can be found in the notes for Vol. 18 Pink Floyd, which was the first release in our series transferred from Millard s original master tapes:

http://www.dimeadozen.org/torrents-details.php?id=667745&hit=1
http://www.dimeadozen.org/torrents-details.php?id=667750&hit=1

Chick Corea & Herbie Hancock, Greek Theatre, Los Angeles, CA, July 9, 1978

We were saddened to hear of the passing of jazz great Chick Corea, so this week we dip into the Millard archive to pay tribute to him with this truly outstanding recording from the Greek Theatre in 1979.

From there, the stage is reset to augment the band and Corea leads them through a set of exceptional performances, including long forays into "Mad Hatter Rhapsody" and "Spanish Fantasy." Corea's wife Gayle Moran also takes the spotlight leading and singing "I Loved You Then, I Love You Now."

While we routinely wax on about the quality of Millard's audience recordings, this one is truly extraordinary, approaching official release standards, no doubt aided by exceptional sound at the outdoor venue, an ideal taping location and Mike's skills and rig. The respectful crowd helps

can you imagine a modern audience being this quiet when an artist introduces a song? Samples provided.

If you're a Corea or Hancock fan, you're in for a treat. If you are merely a Millard devotee, you'l want to hear this one for pure audio excellence alone. Juicy Sonic Magic indeed.

Here's what Jim R recalled about seeing Corea at the Greek 1978:

Mike Millard and I attended the Chick Corea & Herbie Hancock concert at The Greek Theater on July 9, 1978. Being a laid back show, it was easy getting Mike's equipment in.

We sat in row K which is 9-10 rows back. The Greek Theatre is open air with capacity around 5900, very similar to the Universal Amphitheater, which at the time was open air before they put a roof on it in 1982 through its eventual teardown in 2013. Both venues offered excellent acoustics. The sound quality for this show was excellent.

Just to give you a little background of the shows Mike and I attended featuring the Jazz/ Jazz Fusion genre: We recorded Return To Forever in 1977 (Vol. 41 in the Lost and Found series). We recorded Chick with Stanley Clarke in November 1978. And solo tours/shows featuring Al DiMeola, Stanley Clarke and even Lenny White all within a year or so.

The Corea show at the Greek was wonderful. There was some amazing jamming going on. I took the night off from taking pictures.

I hope you enjoy this one as much as Mike and I did.

###

JEMS is proud to join with Rob, Jim R, Barry G, Ed F and others to release Millard's historic recordings and to help set the record straight about the man himself.

We can t thank Rob enough for reconnecting with Jim and putting his trust in our Millard reissue campaign. He kept Mike s precious tapes under wraps for two decades, but once Rob learned of our methods and stewardship, he agreed to contribute the Millard DATs and cassettes to the program. Our releases would not be nearly as compelling without Jim s memories, photos and other background contributions. As many of you have noted, the stories offer an entertaining complement to Mike s incredible audio documents.

This week we again recognize the invaluable assistance of Professor Goody and mjk5510 in helping us ready this show for release. Thanks for being part of the JEMS team.

Finally, cheers to the late, great Mike the MICrophone. His work never ceases to impress. May he rest in peace.

BK for JEMS

concert at Pasadena Civic Auditorium in 1979. Mike and I became friends and we traded some tapes together.
http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Millard

Mike had a few Jazz recordings and was an avid Stevie Wonder fan though he didn't want people to know it. Since
Mike was best known for his legendary Led Zepelin, Pink Floyd, and Rolling Stones recordings, he feared knowledge
of his Jazz recordings would hurt his reputation. As far as I know, only myself and Maybe one other friend of mine
were ever allowed to make copies of his Jazz recordings. This all but guarantees this recording has never been
traded before, or circulated on any of these types of recording sites.

It's been 20+ years since Mike's passing and I've received many persistent requests to work this concert up,
master it, and release it. This is an amazing concert with great 'Mike Millard" sound quality. Please enjoy.

Mike Millard, 1990, RIP

Notes:
It was 25 years ago the last time I listened to this concert and I completely forgot how good it was. Just the names
on the title alone made it special, but I was in for a much bigger surprise. I had always remembered the concert as
Chick Corea, Stanley Clarke, and Lenny White with Al Jarreau. But when I started mastering this recording, I realized
it wasn't Lenny White, but was Tony Williams. Realizing that this recording has the late Tony Williams is what my son
would call an "HCU" (Huge Come-Up) and makes it even more rare and more special than I had remembered. The second HCU
was the concert itself. After listening to it 25 years later, I had forgotten how incredibly great this concert is.
Where else would you ever hear Al Jarreau performing a non-Vocalese version of Spain two years before he recorded it
himself and made it a huge hit.

This recording comes from the tape collection of Mike Millard (see Wiki page). I met Mike in line at a Stevie Wonder
concert at Pasadena Civic Auditorium in 1979. Mike and I became friends and we traded some tapes together.
http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Millard

Mike had a few Jazz recordings and was an avid Stevie Wonder fan though he didn't want people to know it. Since
Mike was best known for his legendary Led Zepelin, Pink Floyd, and Rolling Stones recordings, he feared knowledge
of his Jazz recordings would hurt his reputation. As far as I know, only myself and Maybe one other friend of mine
were ever allowed to make copies of his Jazz recordings. This all but guarantees this recording has never been
traded before, or circulated on any of these types of recording sites.

It's been 20+ years since Mike's passing and I've received many persistent requests to work this concert up,
master it, and release it. This is an amazing concert with great 'Mike Millard" sound quality. Please enjoy.

Mike Millard, 1990, RIP

Source mix Notes:
Source 1 and 2 are essentially the same except from different CD rips. barkndog's source is a cleaner CD rip than damhippy's. damhippy's source has occasional digital glitches and skipped sections. barkndog's 
source has added fades and sometimes fractions of a second less material at the start and end of tracks than damhippy's source. The audio does not run continuously as all the tracks have cuts in between.

At the end of damhippy's source, you can clearly hear the radio announcer say "ici radio Canada" aka, the French version of CBC radio so this is definitely FM and not a soundboard.

I used damhippy's source as the foundation and started off trying to cut out the skipped sections to restore continuity. Then by track 4 the glitches became more frequent. I started splicing in the barkndog source for almost the entirety of Tracks 4, 5, and 6 except for the faded starts and ends. I did this seamlessly, 
which was not particularly difficult because the sources are almost identical. The only minor liberty I took was not leaving a blank gap between Tracks 2 and 3 because the applause (almost) makes it sound 
continuous, and adding about a second of silence between the other tracks.

EDITING NOTES

I transfered this to CDr 3-4 years ago from my master tape that I recorded when it was broadcast in 1991. Musically, it was an awesome show, but it had a lot of tape hiss, which was a major distraction. Having just got Adobe Audition 2.0, I decided to practice using the hiss reduction filter and I'm really happy with the results. The vast majority of hiss has been removed without negatively affecting the nuances of the original source.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
COMMENTS

Do I really need to sell this show? Oh, alright then I will. First, the sound quality is superb as it's from my master cassette. It has
a wonderful, warm analog low end that will give your speakers a nice workout. Secondly, I've seen this show circlating on quite
a few lists, but they are often incomplete - this is the complete FM broadcast. And then there's the show itself, which is just killer -
especially with the 1970s Return to Forever medley kicking things off. And finally - Frank Gambale :-)

The sound quality of the two sources is very similar but not identical. Source 1 (unclewolfi) is the primary source for this extended edition because source 2 has fades between the many of the tracks. Source 2 is missing Trace Dance whereas source 1 is missing the final ~17 minutes of the show. Source 1 had a sampling frequency of 48 kHz whereas source 2 was sampled at 44.1 kHz. Using TAudioConverter, the tracks from source 1 were combined and converted to 44.1 kHz. The combined file of source 1 and the last track of source 2 were then imported into Audacity. From UR website:

 The evening was a series of elegantly choreographed duets between two sympathetic players on fundamentally asymmetrical instruments. With its range, sustain and volume, the piano wins a fair fight every time. Like an elephant dancing with a gazelle, the only way it works is if the elephant is careful.

Some of Corea's best playing has been in duets (see his work with Gary Burton for details.) His strength lies in a virtuosity and fluency

he is a world-class listener with the ability to immediately comment on his counterpart's musical ideas. His weakness, like that of many living legends, is a tendency to sound too much like a facile imitation of himself, is held in check when he is working with an equal like Fleck.

And Fleck is an amazing player, a technical virtuoso who has mastered and transcended the limitations of his instrument. His ability to trade off melodic lines with Corea was impressive, and he nimbly filled the spaces left in the arrangements. When Fleck was alone on stage at the beginning of the encore, the subtlety of his playing shone. When Corea joined him the overtones of the banjo were lost in the lush harmonic brilliance of the piano.

together, these two master musicians weave duets out of staggering virtuosity creating mind-blowing magic performances. Says B_la: _every time Chick and I have played together it has been an extraordinary experience. I have to go beyond my best to hang with Chick!_ Chick Corea's groundbreaking band Return To Forever launched the fusion era of the '70s. His work with flamenco great Paco de Lucia led to the formation of Touchstone, a band whose fiery Latinismo music has bridged the world of flamenco and jazz. His Piano Concerto No. 2 headlined the Vienna's Mozart Celebrations this year. Chick's whole career is the stuff of jazz lore, an amalgamation of influential, limit-stretching, genre-bending musical experiences that have garnered him 12 Grammy awards and legions of fans worldwide. B_la Fleck, considered the premiere banjo player in the world, lives to improvise and loves to work with unexpected musical fusions. Fleck has won 8 Grammys and is the only musician to be nominated for Grammys in jazz, bluegrass, pop, country, gospel, composition and world music categories. (from the Planet Bluegerass Website)

This is part of Chick's nearly 2 month long 75th birthday residency at the Blue Note. A few things seem to be up on youtube from bits and pieces of a few shows, but I think this will be the first complete set from a night.
As you can imagine and will hear, this is really a special pairing that results in a great performance. It was the first of 3 duet nights (Herbie Hancock for night 2, and Gonzalo Rubalcaba for night 3). Chick referred to this night as a Premiere because he and Brad have apparently not played together before this. I'm certainly hoping the experience is repeated and more properly documented. The playing and possibilities with these 2 are phenomenal.Green Dolphin will knock socks off.
I'm hoping more of the nights from this whole run at the Blue Note might pop up from others. It didn't seem that this show was being officially recorded or filmed, as things had been at a Chick's residency when he turned 60. Really hoping to hear the Return to Forever meets Mahavishnu shows that close out this run. In the meantime, we can enjoy this.
Please support these great artists by purchasing their officially released material and by paying to see them live.

comments:
another from the concerts, tours and bands not heard in etree dept. In the extremely busy and active career of Chick Corea, this was one of the last bands he played in (Maybe even the last) before he found and stuck with an obscure little band called Return to Forever. Actually, Corea hasn't played in many obscure bands at all, this May be his most obscure of all, since it was only together for one tour, and not a very long one. I think this is also Chick's first band where he was bandleader, since a year earlier he was keyboard player/sideman for the God of Jazz himself, Miles Davis. This is probably the most avant-garde Corea I've ever heard, and the Miles influence is rather hefty even without a trumpet in this group. This couldn't be more different music than the carefully structured music of RTF. It's also to help celebrate one of the greatest 40 year careers anyone's ever had. If Chick Corea isn't in the jazz hall of fame, they need to rebuild it. He is clearly right up there with Miles and Coltrane as a musical pioneer and legendary concert performer, selling out concerts in 1969 and 2008 and not doing it with very much cheese jazz. Chick does play some of that, but not in here or any of my many Chick posts. He does like to use alot of
synthesizer with RTF, but not here, this is piano Chick, much like my 1972 RTF post. Nothing with Anthony Braxton in it sounds like RTF, including this show.

Neither Chick Corea nor Gary Burton needs any introduction, so I will dispense with
that.

As for the concert and the pairing, its like Mozart Meets Bebop, sort of a cross
between chamber music and jazz. This is thinking person's jazz, the kind of jazz
you'll put on Sunday morning while drinking coffee.

This is a small, quiet auditorium--you could hear a pin drop. Thats the good news.
The bad news is that this is a quiet small, quiet auditorium--you could hear a pin
drop. So every clap, cough or laugh is quiet audible, over any music. I really
didn't want to spend the 2 hours to compress and edit the applause out, and the
crowd was nice enought to let the musicians finish each song before clapping,
so I took the unusual step for me to redact all applause. So this will play
ike a classicalconcert. If you find my mastering technique on this gig offends you,
then don't download this and move on. STFU. Also, those green rechargeable
batteries failed at the 1:36 mark, so if you want the last ten minutes of the
concert, call up Al Gore. Upped on the Dime, March 2011.--Regards, Scooter.

CE_notes:
June 13, 2016 by SURAYA MOHAMED 
Sometimes big-name artists need special attention. But in this case, it wasn't because they've been jazz pioneers and i Nov tors since the 1960s and are considered to be founding fathers of jazz fusion, not to mention two of the most important jazz figures performing today. It's not because they've collectively recorded more than 100 albums and won 29 Grammy Awards. The agitation was because both of their instruments couldn't fit behind Bob Boilen's Tiny Desk.

There were logistical hurdles to overcome before the jazz giants' arrival. We had to move the desk to make a bigger stage. Piano movers hauled the 900-pound Yamaha C7 grand piano from our first-floor performance studio up the freight elevator to the fourth-floor Tiny Desk area. But weeks of meticulous measuring and planning paid off when the rented vibes were delivered and just fit alongside the piano.

Gary Burton and Chick Corea were in town for the 2016 NEA Jazz Masters Concert. The NEA Jazz Masters fellowship is the highest honor our nation bestows on jazz artists. Each year, the program honors a select few living legends who have made exceptional contributions to the advancement of jazz. Burton was a newly appointed 2016 recipient, while Corea received the honor in 2006.

These friends first played together 44 years ago, when they recorded their very first album, Crystal Silence. In his autobiography, Gary Burton tells the story:

We set aside three days for the recording. Except for ... one tune in Munich, Chick and I hadn't worked together before Berlin, so we figured we would need a fair amount of time to choose songs and finalize arrangements. But to our amazement, it all went incredibly fast. We would spend Maybe twenty minutes creating an arrangement, and then record. We did every song in just one take, except that we required a second spin through Senor Mouse.
The record was finished in just a few hours, and the two realized they had a unique musical chemistry with the ability to anticipate each other's improvisational ideas. That album went on to become a classic: flawless yet fresh and forever new.

A few thousand concerts later, the jazz masters showed up at NPR HQ to perform a concert at our newly expanded Tiny Desk. On this day, it had been almost two years since Chick Corea and Gary Burton had played together - the longest break they'd ever had. But once again, their remarkable ability to connect was demonstrated in two songs they play together all the time.

Many Thanks To JEMS

The great Stan Gutoski. R.I.P.

Stan recorded hundreds of shows in and around the Seattle area starting in 1972 and kept taping for over five decades.
He was famous for recording shows on a Tandberg full-track mono reel to reel, and his masters of Led Zeppelin,
Bruce Springsteen, The Who, David Bowie, CSNY, and Joni Mitchell are some of the best '70s recordings of those artists.

What is less widely known about Stan is that he was equally committed to recording radio broadcasts on his home reel to reel which was a Revox B77.
If any local Seattle station was broadcasting a live concert or carrying a syndicated concert series, Stan fired up the recorder,
sometimes going to sleep with an alarm to wake him up to flip the tape (his job in the postal service required him to report to work very early).
He also set up a timer system to record broadcasts when he couldn't be there to start the deck.

Stan made over 200 radio recordings, some on 10" reels that are packed with music and interviews.
Those reels were sitting idle in the JEMS Archive for years until our friends at KRW_CO volunteered to transfer them.
We were only too happy to let a team whose work we admire take possession of the radio reels and bring Stan's tireless late-night efforts into the digital age.

Historic. What else can you say. Not too many times that these 2 icons play together publicly in this duo format. Here they were to mark Chick's 75th birthday. This was a one night event (2 sets-so if anyone got set 2, please share it!) before 4 nights of RTF meets Mahavishnu with presumably more electric keys from Chick and a rhythm section of Victor Wooten and Lenny White (Lenny was seated nearby at this show).Same sharing request goes out to anyone with a recording of these 4 nights.
These guys obviously have an amazing amount of regard and affection for each other and, as previously mentioned, a shared history. Therefore, the emphasis here was on fun and creation. You'll hear Chick say Welcome to our living room. and that was the feeling. The audience were guests at a private jam between 2 amazing artists. This was a tough show to record due to the packed to the rafters house and close quarters with others. Therefore, you'll hear occasional coughs, catcalls, tableware clinks, and waitresses. Despite all of that, it's a great listen. I've split the flac files in such a way that you can eventually edit out the applause and artist comments between tracks if you'd choose to just hear the performances. Chick said he was giving himself a birthday present with Some day My Prince Will Come by having his wife sing with him and John (jokes of course about them both being her former employers). Gayle has always been an aquired taste for some. She's obviously not, to my knowledge, a current performer. I'm relating that because she gamely goes for it in the verses of Prince, but her chops are not what they once might have been. If that's a problem for anyone, John and Chick more than make up in their comping and soloing for anything. Chick was very happy with this, at any rate. It seems there May eventually be some official releases coming from this lengthy Blue Note residency, so please support the artists by purchasing them and their other commercially released material.

Chris Joris is vooral bekend als percussionist, maar hij is ook componist en bandleider. Met zijn New Experience was hij in 1997 al met veel succes op Jazz Middelheim. De band heeft een nieuwe samenstelling, maar de aanpak van Joris blijft dezelfde.

01.

Ari Hoenig (born on November 13, 1973 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania), is a jazz drummer, composer and educator known for his unusual and intense approach to drumming emphasizing complex rhythms in direct harmony with other group members. Ari is widely noted particularly for his drumming not being relegated to just keeping tempo, or being a side issue to the music he plays in, but rather for elevating drumming as an indispensable part of the performance. 
Hoenig is also known for his unique ability to modify the pitch of a drum by using drum sticks, mallets, and even parts of his body (such as his hands and elbows). Using this technique, he can play any note in the chromatic scale, virtually any melody, and even improvise on a chord structure in the same way as any other instrumentalist would. 
Hoenig was born into a family of classically trained musicians. His father being a choral conductor and mother a violinist, he was exposed to classical and folk music at an early age. He played both piano and violin as a child, then rock and metal drums as a teen before settling into jazz and improvised music. 
Ari has recorded written and produced 14 cd s as a leader. He has written and published 3 educational books, 4 educational DVD s and a songbook. Currently, his group tours worldwide and performs regularly at the legendary New York jazz club Smalls. Ari is currently touring and performing with his trio of Nitai Hershkovits on piano and Or Bareket on bass as well as his nonet and quartet which he won the BMW Welt competition in 2013. Other artists Hoenig has performed or recorded with include Shirley Scott, Jean Michel Pilc, Mike Stern, Kenny Werner, Joshua Redman, Wayne Krantz, Kurt Rosenwinkel, Richard Bona, Chris Potter, Toots Thielemans, Pat Martino, Billy Childs.

Chris Potter
A world-class soloist, accomplished composer and formidable bandleader, saxophonist Chris Potter has emerged as a leading light of his generation. Down Beat called him One of the most studied (and copied) saxophonists on the planet while Jazz Times identified him as a figure of international renown. Jazz sax elder statesman Dave Liebman called him simply, one of the best musicians around, a sentiment shared by the readers of Down Beat in voting him second only to tenor sax great Sonny Rollins in the magazine s 2008 Readers Poll.
A potent improvisor and the youngest musician ever to win Denmark s Jazzpar Prize, Potter s impressive discography includes 15 albums as a leader and sideman appearances on over 100 albums. He was nominated for a Grammy Award for his solo work on In Vogue, a track from Joanne Brackeen s 1999 album Pink Elephant Magic, and was prominently featured on Steely Dan s Grammy-winning album from 2000, Two Against Nature. He has performed or recorded with many of the leading names in jazz, such as Herbie Hancock, Dave Holland, John Scofield, the Mingus Big Band, Jim Hall, Paul Motian, Dave Douglas, Ray Brown and many others.

Trying to eliminate the discs and clear shelf space lately often has me in a section relating to Oregon, and here's another that I'll get circulating again. Collin Walcott (CO of Codona) was the percussionist, but really another multi instrumentalist and composer in Oregon during their first decade until his untimely death in a van accident while touring in 1984. Don Cherry (DO), was of course an associate of Ornette Coleman's, who did many avant-garde projects, but also headed a little more towards the musical mainstream with a few things released by Atlantic and A&M Horizon in the mid to late 70's. Nana Vasconcelos (NA) was another in the line of Brazilian percussionist that included Airto Moreira and Dom Um Romao to break more internationally. That first happened in the company of ECM labelmate Egberto Gismonti. He also had a prominent association with Pat Metheny in the early 80's.
Codona released 3 albums on ECM every other year between 1979 and 1983. The material in this show mainly relates to that first album. ECM was pretty cool back at this time, as they often putting together combinations of their artists into new projects like this. Magico with Gismonti, Jan Garbarek, and Charlie Haden
Gateway with John Abercrombie, Dave Holland, and Jack DeJohnette

and one with Terje Rypdal, Miroslav Vitous, and DeJohnette are other examples from this general timeframe.
This show was upped here 3 other times beginning in 2005 with KnutMS and blueschief, but it hasn't been here since a 2011 seed by Jack Warner, that got banned according to the dimebot archive because the mod nightshifted indicated that "there was insufficient information because Codona never played at Willisau". I checked the Willisau Festival archive, and this show definitely did happen ther on that date, but apparently not under the name Codona, which May not yet have been chosen by the time festival promotion was prepared. The performers were listed in promo materials in the archive as both "The Don Cherry Group" and alternately by all 3 of their names a la "Crosby, Stills, and Nash".
My copy came to me in a cd-r trade, but might in some way relate to one of the 3 times it was up here. Thanks to the trader who made this available to me, and to those who first recorded it and passed it along to the rest of us.

comments:
When I went searching for a setlist to this, I found out much to my shock,
this trio has a released live CD- but it's from 1990 at Nightstage! A nice place to do that for them, I've gotta get that released disc. I wasn't able to find any info on this concert at all, but I thought enough of it despite a good 1st transfer to disc to just spare you all CD lineage details on this one entirely and do a fresh new transfer. I think this may be a little better, it needed some patching of distorting mike chord on one side, not too much of it though, and now this is a very enjoyable recording of a very good acoustic guitar trio. The Next Generation of Al/John/Paco trio here, since Coryell was briefly in that trio with John and Paco in 79, then 81 and 83 was with Al/John/Paco, then there was the guitarist who blew DiMeola away at right around the age (if not even younger) then when Al first did that. If Al DiMeola says you're a great guitarist, that says alot, and Lagrène is really good, worthy of such great company. This trio is every bit as good (not quite the same) as AJP trio. This was a very good concert. Other than a very nice upload from Phila several years ago, I haven't seen any other recordings of this trio (in any quality). The tape copy had a few loud sounds from a mike chord shorting out. All but a little of the least noticable
parts of that has been eliminated here by "monoizing" mostly very short sections, a couple as long as maybe 20 seconds. I managed to do it so it's not very noticable (either monoizing or the shorting out sound), I reduced a few loud claps, and it sounds better than ever for its torrential unveiling. I didn't record this show, so maybe the master has been posted, but I haven't heard of this show being around from any other source. It's one worth hearing many times over, no jarring noises left any more. most of this has no shorting out or noises, and the recording was fairly close up.
With Al still touring (with another trio most recently), I thought this might be a good time to hear some very good Acoustic Al with a couple of other guitar monsters. This was near the beginning of a five week tour for this trio. the introduction and tape flip are very slightly cut, hardly even noticable, thanks to P. J. for recording this show. He did a good job, and if he ever hears this remaster and hasn't done something similar himself to this recording, I think he would enjoy hearing it without any loud distortion noises in it. Only a few short portions where it's still there, but not the loud parts (I did not "minimize or reduce" any of the distortion parts, only monoizing sections where it was loud, so the music volume continuity is maintained because all the mike chord shorting out noise was in one side.
the opening set needed alot more help than this one did)

Dave Brubeck Quartet
November 9, 1961
Gruga Halle
Essen, Germany

-REMASTERED-

The Dave Brubeck Quartet at Gruga Halle , Essen, Germany, November 1961.

From two German radio broadcasts (TT 68:11) taped by an old friend of mine back in 1961 in the Netherlands. Monaural, no hi-fi, but pretty good

remember: no cable etc. in those days, and radio signals could become distorted by e.g. mopeds passing by in the street! Back then we grew up in the same neighbourhood in a city close to the German border. Some 15 years or so ago I borrowed this tape from him and made a perfect copy of it.

Don't think this has ever been re-broadcast or has surfaced anywhere in any form! If it's been here on Dime before, please let me know!

(In a trade, I once got a copy of a Dave Brubeck concert from the same venue - presumably originated from Dime - but from the year before April 2, 1960.)

Enjoy!

Combos from the Thompson Jazz Studies Program are joined by NEA Jazz
Master Dave Holland, pianist and composer Nikki Illes, and trumpetist
Nick Smart for a spectacular night of music. Featuring original
compositions by Holland!

Dave Holland is a bassist, composer and bandleader whose passion for
musical expression and dedication to creating consistently innovative
music have propelled a professional career of more than 50 years,
multiple Grammy awards and the title of NEA Jazz Master in 2017.

Holland stands as a guiding light on acoustic and electric bass, having
grown up in an age when musical genresjazz, rock, funk, avant-garde,
folk, electronic music and othersblended freely together to create new
musical pathways. He was a leading member of a generation that helped
usher jazz bass playing from its swing and post-bop legacy to the
vibrancy and multidiscipline excitement of the modern era, extending the
instrument's melodic, expressive capabilities. Holland's virtuosic
technique and rhythmic feel, informed by an open-eared respect of a
formidable spread of styles and sounds, is widely revered and remains
much in demand. To date, his playing can be heard on hundreds of
recordings, with more than thirty as a leader under his own name.

Notes: This was 8 songs by 8 different Jazz combos. Song 1 and 8 had Dave on bass and Nikki Illes Piano and trumpet Nick Smart. Dave, Nikki and Nick had 1-2 of the Jazz combos to either play with or conduct them. John Gunther played Sax and Paul Romaine on Song 1 and 8 too. All Star Night!

Notes (only in Dutch):
De legendarische bassist Dave Holland zette de jongste jaren een samenwerking op met de grote Flamenco-gitarist Pepe Habichuela. Het is muziek waarvan een grote kracht uitgaat. De solo's zijn adembenemend en alle grenzen, talen en stijlen lijken erin op te lossen.

De 63-jarige Engelse bassist en bandleader Dave Holland treedt al gedurende bijna vijf decennia op. Eind van de jaren zestig werd hij ontdekt door Miles Davis, toen hij optrad in de bekende Londense jazzclub Ronnie Scott. Hij speelde mee op Miles Davis-albums zoals Bitches Brew en Big Fun, waarna zijn pad hem van de grenzen van de vrije improvisatie naar zijn hedendaagse ensembles leidde. Hij werkte met heel wat bekende namen samen van Thelonious Monk tot Anthony Braxton, van Stan Getz tot Cassandra Wilson, van Chick Corea tot Pat Metheny, van Bill Frisell tot Herbie Hancock. Zijn werk varieert van solo performances tot big band werk. Met gitarist John Scofield, drummer Al Foster en saxofonist Joe Lovano vormde hij het succesrijke kwartet ScoLoHoFo. Sinds 1999 leidt hij een kwintet. Met saxofonist Chris Potter, vibrafonist Steve Nelson, trombonist Robin Eubanks en drummer Nate Smith vormt hij een ijzersterke band. Holland is een meester van toon en ritme, zijn muziek is rijk en caleidoscopisch.

Dave Holland leerde Flamenco gitarist Pepe Habichuela kennen via een gemeenschappelijke vriend, Mario Pacheco, eigenaar van een platenlabel in Spanje. Hij dacht dat we het plezierig zouden vinden om samen te spelen. Hij had gelijk, vertelt Dave Holland. We speelden ons eerste concert in 2007. De sfeer was uitstekend en ik hield van de muziek die we maakten. Er volgden nog concerten. Het was een ontroerende ervaring. Maar ik wilde geen fusionproject doen. Dan verlies je aan beide kanten iets. Ik wilde de culturele identiteit van die muziek respecteren. Pepe moest mijn leraar zijn. Pepe is 100 procent flamenco, dat is zijn wereld. Mijn muziek daarmee mengen zou zijn muziek devalueren.

Ik kende wel muziekelementen die bij flamenco passen zoals tango, rumba, buleria. Maar hoe dieper je gaat, hoe meer je de complexiteit van al die dansvormen ontdekt. Je moet de finesses goed verstaan. Ik bezocht Spanje drie keer om die muziek te leren. Ik wilde die muziek recht doen, omdat ik er zoveel respect voor had. Het is een zeer beschermde kunst. Dat heeft te maken met de zigeuneridentiteit en cultuur. Die mensen werden erg gediscrimineerd. Muziek is uiterst belangrijk voor hen. Dat zit heel diep.

Pepe Habichuela is een telg van een grote flamencodynastie, de Habichuelas. Hij behoort tot de generatie van Paco de Luc a, Camar n de la Isla, Enrique Morente, Manolo Sanl car, musici die deze kunstvorm enorm populair maakten. Hij begon in de flamencogrotten van Granada en belandde dan in de caf s van Madrid. In de jaren zeventig maakte hij twee historische opnamen: Despegando en Homenaje a D. Antonio Chac n. Maar zijn avontuurlijke geest bracht hem al vlug buiten de afgelijnde paden van de flamenco. Hij speelde met free jazz legende Don Cherry en zette experimenten op waarbij hij flamenco met klassieke Indische muziek versmolt.

notes:
The late and much missed MM provided this cassette copy (TDK SA-X90 with Dolby C) of his now-lost cassette not long after this show took place. He May have recorded the show himself, although if he did so it is odd that he did not note the exaact date and venue on the cassette's J-card. It is possible he acquired this recording from someone else, or that he was simply in too much of a hurry when he labeled his tape or this copy--although, musician and music teacher that he was--he did find the time to carefully note the names of almost all the tunes.

While the musicians have each been affiliated with the Berklee College of Music in Boston, the sometimes noisy crowd and occasional clanking of dishes and glasses suggests that this recording was made in a Boston club and not in a Berklee auditorium. It May have been billed as the Lagzlo Gardony Trio with guest David Liebman, given that Gardony, Vitous, and Froman recorded an album under Gardony's name the following year (https://www.discogs.com/Laszlo-Gardony-The-Secret/release/2389334).

There is no indication in the following sources that this performance has been officially released.

I just recently seeded a Sancious show from the Main Point in Bryn Mawr, PA. That got a pretty favorable reaction, so I'm reacting to a few comments from that show by seeding another Sancious and Tone show that sounds really good. This, the Bryn Mawr show, and the 1976 WLIR broadcast from Roslyn, NY are the best sounding live artifacts from this band that I know of. This particular show seems to date to the period in between Sancious and Tone's 2 Epic Records releases. All 3 of the shows I mentioned contain at least one song that never made it to an album. That song here is the final track, Energy.
This is the earlier Tone band that didn't feature the vocals heard on the Bryn Mawr show and the later True Stories and Just As I Thought albums.They were a powerhouse Trio, and I saw them at this time (and later with the vocal focus). I recall audiences being wowed by Sancious switching from keys to guitar, and basically tearing it up on each of them. Mentioning again for anyone not familiar with Sancious that he became known in Springsteen's E Street Band, but that association ended on Born to Run. His Epic debut was produced by Billy Cobham, and he did extensive side work with Stanley Clarke, Lenny White, and Narada Michael Walden while with Tone. Since the early 80's, he's appeared with Jack Bruce, Jon Anderson, Santana, Peter Gabriel, Sting, Seal, and others. He's also done a few things in the last 10-15 years under his own name again, but none of them has gotten very wide attention.
I know I've had this show on the disc I've used for these files for many years. I don't know if this came to me in a download here or in a cd-r snail mail trade, but big thanks to whoever made the show available to me, and to those who first recorded it and distributed it. I also wanted to mention that etree info about this show, and some comments from the Bryn Mawr seed, make it seem that both shows had circulated in pretty poor form with digital issues and spotty sound. That wasn't the case with either of these uploads, and I'm happy if better versions might've now gotten out there through these shares.
Please support musical artists by paying to see them live, and by purchasing their commercially released material.

Here's something that's probably been up on the tracker before, but doesn't seem to be here now. It's a day or 2 away from the 39th anniversary of this performance. Paco and Larry are gone, but John is happily still here and still able to show his stuff and great artistry.
Seeig the re-constituted Dixie Dregs the other night on Long Island reminded me that the first time I ever saw Steve Morse was as the solo opener for the the Guitar Trio of McLaughlin, Paco, and Al DiMeola in LA in 1983 or 84. That memory caused me to re-visit some of the shows I had of Mclaughlin in that basic configuration and led me to this particular performance.
Of course, it's well known that Larry was having personal issues that led to Dimeola famously joining up, but the set of players heard here was the original idea.
Thanks to whoever originally shared this recording with me, and the taper.
For anyone interested, I do have about a 20 minute audio recording of 3 tracks supposedly from Le Castelet, FR on 7/25/1976 that is a quartet of the 3 featured here plus Philip Catherine.I'm not 100% convinced about the accuracy of that date or the source, but if anyone knows anything about that performance and assure me that it won't be banned as video sourced, please indicate that in the comments section, and I'll seed that too.
Please support the artists by paying for their commercially released material, and pay to see John play, if and when he does in the future.

Here are a few sets(All I have) from 1982's Company week in NYC. These were recorded by me on a Sony TCS-310 about 12 feet from the musicians, so the sound is clear, if not exactly hi-fi.

This was my first exposure to most of these players, and I was totally blown away. The fire-breathing duo of Brotzmann and Maslak is a performance I will NEVER forget. I only wish I had video so you could all see Maslak rolling around on the floor still maniaclly blowing his horn, while off to the side, John Zorn was crouched, grinning from ear to ear. 

Derek Bailey, Fred Frith, Bill Laswell, Joelle Leandre, Peter Brotzmann, Keshavan Maslak, John Zorn, and Cyro Baptiste were the participants during this Company week, and during the nights I was there, Bailey called mostly smaller groupings. Découvrez ou redécouvrez la programmation des Nocturnes du Mercredi 31 octobre 2012. Une émission dans laquelle vous pouvez retrouver l'invitée de Georges Lang : Diana Krall!

Diana Krall est venue il y a quelques jours dans le studio des Nocturnes de RTL pour nous présenter son nouvel album "Glad Rag Doll". Délaissant quelque peu le jazz, la pianiste et chanteuse canadienne a cherché dans le répertoire américain des années 1920-30 des chansons entendues dans sa famille et qu'elle a reprises en studio, sous la direction du producteur de légende T. Bone Burnett. Le résultat est tout à fait surprenant, tout comme la pochette du CD d'ailleurs qui nous montre une Diana Krall très sensuelle dans une tenue légère de chanteuse de revue, elle s'en explique d'ailleurs au micro de Georges Lang dans un entretien que vous pourrez entendre après le concert de l'artiste enregistré sur la scène du Grand Studio. Diana Krall parle sans détour de sa vie de mère de famille (elle est la maman de jumeaux dont le père s'appelle Elvis Costello), de ses aspirations musicales, de sa jeunesse passée dans une petite ville de la Colombie Britannique, de son amour pour la musique de Django Reinhardt et Stéphane Grapelli, de sa rencontre avec Neil Armstrong et de son interprétation de "Fly me to the moon" le jour des funérailles de l'astronaute américain à Washington. Dans la première heure de l'émission, écoutez le concert de Diana Krall entourée de musiciens exceptionnels, puis découvrez une artiste qui répond aux questions de Georges Lang dans l'intimité du studio des Nocturnes de RTL, jusqu'à trois heures du matin.

A noter que Diana Krall chantera le 3 novembre au Palais des Congrès de Strasbourg et le 21 novembre au Palais des Congrès de Paris.

Performed on what would have been DG's 78's birthday, organized by Jazz Forum Arts Presents. Tickets were $25.00. The core band (West, Roker, Harris) is joined by a rotating cast of trumpet virtuoso's and other musicians. Hopefully, it's clear who's on stage during which songs.

The late and much missed MM no doubt acquired this recording via a 1980s cassette trade from an unknown source. He made a copy of his now-lost cassette on a Maxell XLII90 cassette using Dolby C not long afterwards. That copy was digitized in 2021, using a refurbished Sony TC WR635S cassette deck and Goldwave. Because the left channel was weaker than the right channel and had acquired some static on track 1 at some point in its travels, the stronger right channel was pasted over the left channel in 2021 to create a true mono presentation of this recording.

I've seeded several Eberhard Weber shows in recent weeks, and this will be the final one that I'll do. This is a show I got in a cd-r trade many years ago. I'm not sure how widely circulated this is, or if it's been on DIME before. It's a bit of an outlier in that there aren't a lot of Weber shows from 1981. I've seen this listed in places as coming from Berlin (is Peltz near Berlin?), and I've seen it as coming from November 5th, rather than 15th. There's also another show involving Weber from this same general time and area in which he's not playing with Colours. If anyone can clear any of that up, please do that in the comments. Let's also remember that Berlin, although partially free, was inside communist East Germany at this time, and there is something I've read that suggests this was a jazz fest behind "the Iron Curtain".
This finds the band playing a similar repertoire to many of their 1979 shows. Does that mean the 1981 date here is wrong? We could be up all night trying to pinpoint these details, so my recommendation is to simply enjoy another fine show from some wonderful musicians.

According to the dimebot archive, this hasn't been up here since 2007, so it's probably about time. Besides, Eberhard Weber just had his 83rd birthday a few days ago. The material in this show seems to come mainly from 2 of his albums, Pendulum and Orchestra.Seven Movements.I've corrected the date from 11-05 to 05-11, as that's what's shown on Paul McCandless's own website. That also reveals the performance to have been part of the "Berlin Jazz Festival".
McCandless and Weber had teamed up by that point for a couple of Weber's albums and projects. McCandless, of course, is the reed player associated with the band Oregon, but he's done lots of work with others, ranging from Jaco Pastorius's Big Band to Bela Fleck and the Flecktones. No dj or audience appears on these tracks, so it's unclear if this was a radio broadcast, so somehow intended for release. In any case, it's a fine recording of 2 great players in a rather rare kind of duo configuration.
My copy of this came in a cd-r trade long ago, but this had been on DIME in 2005 and 2007 via rommedoe and jmgdiscs. I replaced the incomplete St. Louis Blues track from the CD with the complete version from the previous upload.

So here we have now the (imo) MOST COMPLETE VERSION of Ella's Amsterdam concert in February 1961.

CE_notes:
Ella Fitzgerald in The Netherlands: Amsterdam 1961 & Tilburg 1971
1961-02-18 & 1971-05-07

Going 40-50 years back, this is some vintage Ella from:
1961 (tracks 1-9
Concertgebouw Amsterdam 18/19 February - midnight concert) and 1971 (tracks 10-17

Pelikaanhal - Pelican Hall - Tilburg, the Netherlands, 7 May). Dutch radio broadcasts.

The 1961 part was (re)broadcast in the early 1990's, whereas the 1971 part - being originally broadcast in 1972 - was re-broadcast as part of the in memoriam Ella Fitzgerald radio program in 1996. Broadcast announcements: Aad Bos (1961) and Michiel de Ruyter (1971). My tapings of the broadcasts.

As far as I know, these recordings have never surfaced on either LP or CD (not in my latest Lord edition 6.0). The 1961 recording is between the Verve CD Ella Returns To Berlin (11 February) and the bootleg Jazz Door CD from Belgrade (21 February). The 1971 recording is about 10 days before the bootleg CD on Jazz Door (Belgrade, 18 May, but without the Basie band).

The Tilburg recording May be a little less vintage, but Ella is in great form here and the surprises are the tracks with the Count Basie band. In C-Jam Blues: Basie at the piano and soloing by Al Grey and Eddie Lockjaw Davis.

Enjoy!

Personnel:
1961: Lou Levy (p), Herb Ellis (g), Wilfred Middlebrooks (b), Gus Johnson (dr)

From original notes:

Emily plays with Barbara Dennerlein's band taking a number of solos and a featured accompaniment spot, sitting out only on one number. It's great to see Emily display her real art as an accompanist which she often remarked as being what she enjoyed doing the most.

Also there are two TV clips from Australia - 'Tenor Madness' is from May 1989 (Ray Martin Midday Show) and I'm certain that 'How Insensitive' (Tonight with Steve Vizard) was recorded in lat April or very early May 1990 very close to her sad departing of this world on May 4th 1990. 

The DVD has a chapter menu in 4 parts:

Enjoy!
Visit http://www.allthingsemily.com
Keep Emily's wonderful music and spirit alive...

The meeting between Enrico Rava and Fred Hersch brings together two extraordinary musical stories.

Enrico Rava, born in Trieste in 1939, is the best known and most appreciated Italian jazz player on an international level. His frankness, human and artistic, places him outside any framework and makes him a rigorous musician but heedless of conventions. His immediately recognizable poetics, his lyrical and poignant sonority, always supported by an amazing freshness of inspiration, stand out in all his musical adventures.
Rava appeared on the jazz scene in the mid-1960s, quickly establishing himself as one of the finest soloists in European jazz. He was initially inspired by charismatic figures such as Chet Baker and Miles Davis. However, he soon approaches the avant-garde, playing with Gato Barbieri, Don Cherry, Mal Waldron and Steve Lacy. Later, after moving to New York for about ten years, he collaborated with other experimental musicians, including Roswell Rudd, Marion Brown, Cecil Taylor, Carla Bley. Then he gradually found a remarkable individuality approach to the mainstream. Rava's personality is unique for the way he has been able to give excellent results both in the field of research jazz (especially in the first part of his career) and in the wake of tradition.

In the Big Book of Famous Phrases at one point we read "I would not be doing what I do if I had not learned from Fred": words by Brad Mehldau, referring to Fred Hersch, of whom he was a student.
Born in Cincinnati in 1955, Fred Hersch demonstrates a precocious talent for the piano: he has studied it since the age of four and at ten he was already winning national piano competitions. The college years are also those of the discovery of jazz. The first important collaboration was with Art Farmer (the meetings with Joe Henderson, Stan Getz, Toots Thielemans and Janis Siegel stand out), but since the beginning of the Eighties he is already active above all as a leader in the formats that will remain his most regulars: the trio, the duo and the solo piano.
Hersch is a truly unique artist in the jazz scene, with an executive style based on the models of Bill Evans and Herbie Hancock, filtered by acute sensitivity and solid classical preparation. Each episode of his rich discography, as well as every single performance of his, is a moment of profound musical revelation, offered to the listener like a precious gem.

As promised yesterday, I've looked into my Five Peace Band shows to find something that sounded good to add to the recent shows from Boston and Leverkusen. This one fits chronologically between the 2 of them, and this one still finds Vinnie Colaiuta on the drum stool. None of the shows I have are FM's or SB's, and this one seemed to be a little bit better sounding than the others. Not sure if this one is more or less common, or if this was ever here on DIME (guessing that it was).
RIP, Chick. Support the other great musicians by purchasing their commercially released material (new John McLaughlin album coming in July, 2021). Thanks to whoever first recorded this show and shared it with me.

An excellent sounding show. The first using my new recorder. There are a few minor flaws, caused mostly by me trying to re-adjust my croakie mics under my collar. I'm sure no one is going to mind. Overall, the recording quality turned out beyond my expectations. This had a lot to do with the audience acting accordingly, by refraining from chatter for the most part.

As for the performance, besides outstanding solos from everyone, I think the band seems a little less aggressive with Brian Blade. As much as I love his playing with Wayne Shorter, I would've preferred Vinnie Colaiuta. Another disappointment, though a very minor one, was the unbelievably short version of "In A Silent Way", an absolute highlight from the live CD. But after almost 2.5 hours of playing, I imagine the guys were tired. Overall, an unbelievable once-in-a-lifetime concert experience, no fusion fan should've missed...Enjoy!!!

Recording Notes:
- This was a very difficult and incredibly stealthy recording situation...I did the best I could given the circumstances. As always, it's better than nothing. 
- If you download this recording and then wind up selling it as a bootleg on-line, I will hunt you down and eat your children. And a continued pox on the scoundrel that did just that to my Clapton/Marsalis recording from earlier this year...total clown-shoes, bubba.

Special Recording Note (aka "A Clumsy Drunk @ the Blue Note"):
- As if being packed into my seat wasn't tough enough to pull off this
recording, I also had the misfortune of being seated right next to a drunken klutz with a weak bladder. Of note...he gets up for a bathroom break right before Chick's solo in "Special Beings"...he returns 2 mins later, banging into me as he squeezes back into his seat...20 seconds later, as he settles himself, he manages to spill a full glass of water all over the table and onto my lap...good times. What makes this all really fun for you, the listener...is that the entire debacle is fairly audible as the music plays on. The only consolation is that he and his buddy left just as "Hymn to Andromeda" begins...which is audible as well...but its brief and the rest of the recording continues uninterrupted.

Performance Notes:
- This show was part of Chick Corea's month-long residency this month at the Blue Note in celebration of his 70th birthday. I'd urge everybody to check the show calender for November and make it out to a show if they are in the area.
- I saw this group at NYC's Rose Theater back i April of '09 and was
thoroughly throttled from the experience. So, the mere thought of the same group flexing their abilities in a place as tiny and packed as the Blue Note made me salivate as I made my ticket purchase weeks in advance. Overall, the show was excellent, albeit...a bit more subdued than the incendiary Rose Theater show 2 years back. My guess is that they were fully aware of the potential of them blowing the walls down of the tiny jazz club and toned-down the set accordingly. They wouldn't want faces melting and people passing out left and right as that's not very good for business...

^)
- Each one of these musicians is a head-liner and legend in their own right and yet are still able to commune with one another in this format without ego diluting the sanctity and message of the music. That, in and of itself, is as rare as each of these musicians are themselves.

Support these artists...buy their CDs...attend their sets...visit their
websites...and dig their craft.

Frank Zappa_1976-02-17 Sporthalle - Cologne, Germany

This audience recording was received in a cassette tape trade in 1981.
Possibly third generation. The quality is slighly below average with
some Wow and Flutter. This copy has No Distortion and is definatly more listenable then the one circulating by Yojimbo & flambay. On the Y & F recording, they have "San Ber'dino" as the last track. I had an additional 12 minutes labled on another tape as being the final portion of this show. It started with Black Napkins and contained another song but not San Ber'dino. So that must be filler for an unnamed show as the sound quality was better and definatly not this show, so it is not included here.

Discovered flaws:

The original folders were reversed, throwing the sets askew. The tracks are now finally presented in the correct order, and the running order of the sets makes much more sense now. Intro tracks have been split, revealing the actual end of the first set and beginning of the second.

D1T1 - 10:59-11:02 - speed/pitch lowers, then raises back up. Cannot repair.

D1T3 - unknown time - various levels raised or lowered where necessary to smooth and even out a couple seconds of music by as much as +/-6db o Separate channels at similar times. Ending properly faded.

The sound is a bit rough at times, revealing the age of the tape. Also, the soundman occasionally has a microphone channel muted, and a couple occasional buzzes resulting from a channel coming on May be a bit jarring. The listener will note that he's still trying to adjust the levels at the very beginning, but it finally comes together pretty quickly. All other levels remain as they were originally found, leaving some of the mix uneven at times, but it seemed to me to be a more musical choice, (as the proximity to a mic could not be changed here, well after the fact. That's physics, folks!)

The pitch was originally approximately 34 cents flat throughout. That has been corrected here.

Thanks to all involved in creating, preserving and sharing this great set for us to discover many years later, leading to this presentation today. The original source was seeded by dsgtrane, which is how I got it back in '05. Special thanks to him! Thanks to twat and ubu as well.

I've been digitizing, and then discarding, cd-r's from many years of trades and downloads. That recently led me to look at some more of the Metheny related stuff on my shelves and this show from very early on. I'd basically forgotten about this particular performance. I got this on DIME in 2010 when it was shared, seemingly for the 2nd and last time it was up here (according to the dimebot archive). It was shared then by a DIME'er going by the user name of araslim. Big thanks to him, and to whoever first recorded this, and those who passed that recording down the line. The only thing I've done to those files was normalizing levels in Audacity, mainly to address balance discrepancies that were particularly noticeable on the 2 solo tracks.
Pat, of course, came to prominence as a member of Gary Burton's groups immediately before starting to release music under his own name. He first did that in the year of this performance, and was still working a bit at that point with Burton. Pat still gives a world of credit to Gary Burton for setting him on the course into the kind of music he'd produce throughout his career. This show is a nice opportunity to hear the 2 of them in a well recorded and played intimate setting. Tracks one and 2 are solo performances by each of the artists, and the rest are then duo tracks. I particularly enjoy hearing a very early run through Pat's September 15th, the beautiful composition he debuted in recorded form a few years after this on the As Falls Wichita album with Lyle Mays.

What follows below are notes from araslim's share in 2010:
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Here's a great duet show that appears to have not been on dime for a couple years. It was seeded as 1976-12-xx, which is how I received it, but when removed from the tracker, the title had been changed to 1976-12-02, so hopefully whatever information was received on the date is correct. I re-named the files and added tags, but didn't make any changes to the music. I don't have any further information on the lineage, I received it in a trade a few years back. A sample is below. Enjoy!

This show was last up here in 2012 according to the bot archive when a user named woessner shared it. Oddly enough, it didn't show up on the bot under either artist's name, or the date. It only came up while searching through the name of the venue.
This is a soundboard that I believe I got in a cd-r snail mail trade. Whoever recorded it or shared it got rid of the majority of any applause or stage chatter. That too was the case in the share that was on DIME from woessner. Given that this all fit on one cd-r, that decision was probably made in the interest of fitting the music on a single disc because it is at about the maximum length (79 minutes or so) that would fit on a cd-r. I've done the best I could with the titles of what was played, but if anyone can help in the instance of my "unknown" titles, please do.
The show appears to have been in support of the Slide Show album that came out on ECM around the time of this gig. That was Ralph and Gary's secong ECM project, and it came 12 or 13 years after their first, Matchbook. Much of the music played here is from Slide Show. I searched to see what I could find about the venue, and there are setlists from some shows played there by other artists in the late 80's, but there was no info about this particular show. Curiously, there don't seem to be any other shares from Ralph and Gary dating to this year when they might have been promoting the new record. This show itself doesn't appear to have circulated very much. I'm one of only 3 people on etree who seem to have it. Now you'll have it too. It's a good one.
Thanks to whoever recorded this, and to whoever made it available to me in trade.

This is a reseed of yet another of those groups formed by individual artists who recorded for ECM in the 1970's. I've recently seeded some shows from Codona and Magico, and Gateway was actually the first of these ECM "supertrios". They also re-convened much later for 2 more albums and more touring. Their first album came out in 75, and there are a few other shows circulating from that time. Glasnostd19 had upped one of them during some toasty summer weather last year (just getting used to saying that now in reference to 2022!). I recall someone voicing the hope then that this particular show would be reseeded at that time, but no one jumped on the request.
This Hamburg show had been up here a few times over a decade ago, and there were a few different versions. The one here is reputedly the "best". It came from Randy Bayers (thanks to him). I'll paste in what I'd found from the dimebot archive below about how he put this together, along with the lineage info from his share. It basically involved a cleaner version he'd picked up in a trade that was missing the final few tracks, and included one track that was inferior to Ian's version (glasnostd19's-thanks to him too). He put Ian's files that were missing from his set along with the better version of Bessie's Blues from Ian too, and Bob's your uncle (in other words, that's what we've got here). I'd burned this to 3 discs when I got it back in 2010-it's a long show-, so I had to include the EAC and TLH steps you'll see in the lineage above to get this up again.
Thanks to anyone left out in the list of those who'd recorded and shared this show along the way. Randy Bayer's 2010 info below:

Although this source is likely also from a cassette or other analog source it has a little less hiss and a little more clarity than glasnostrd19's source. Unfortunately, my source came on only 2 discs and was missing the last 3 tracks, so I've included those last 3 tracks from glasnostrd19's source. In addition, my version of Bessie's Blues was quieter and not very clear, so I've substituted glasnostrd19's source for that track as well. Also, glasnostrd19's source had Ralph's Piano Waltz and Remembering mixed up, so I've switched them. - RandyB Jan. 3, 2010

notes:
Based on the audience reaction to Adams' reference to Saturday night on track 9, it appears that this performance May have been broadcast on a Saturday night. The Italian Soul Note label recorded two LPs worth of material on August 19, 1983 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_at_the_Village_Vanguard_Vol._2), which was a Friday night. The track lists of these LPs do not overlap with the track list of this performance, with the exception of Intentions and Big Alice, and, possibly, of Saturday Night in the Cosmos. A side by side listening comparison of the Intentions on the LP and the one on this broadcast reveals that they are not the same performance of this piece. While the LP versions of Big Alice or Saturday Night in the Cosmos were not available for comparison with track 9, the LP versions are not the same length or sequence as track 9. This evidence suggests that this live broadcast May have taken place the night after Soul Note recorded the material for its two LPs.

George Benson Quartet - Jazz Workshop, Boston 1973-02-27 C.T.I. Era, FM (Jazamo fix) 

A fan of the early 70's C.T.I. Record label, it was a time when I became passionate about all styles of Jazz. I thought I'd share some CTI era artists that have been posted previously in Dime including my fixes. 

Here's a set from George Benson recorded during his early CTI days at the Jazz Workshop by WBCN Radio. This rare set includes his new backup guitarist Earl Klugh who had yet to record his debut lp. It also includes 2 songs Benson never recorded in the studio with the Marvin Gaye Medley , and Cafe Reggio , The later featured at the time on the Shaft soundtrack. I have applied some fixes to this show (see notes), and should anybody has a different source please share. Welcome to Volume 24 of the Inner Voice: Jazz Masters Series featuring a beautiful recording of American jazz pianist, composer and educator Geri Allen.

Allen was the quintessential modern day jazz pianist very much in the conceptual vain of
Keith Jarret, Herbie Hancock and Bill Evans. She was well-versed in all forms of jazz from bop to free. She had a gift for melody that was complimented by expressive spontaneity.
She has a personal style that walked the line of being both challenging and easily accessible.

This is a beautiful soundboard captured at the Festival de Verona, it is missing the last song Stop The World but other than that is an extremely satisfying listen.

Allen passed away in 2017 of complications due to cancer.

Thanks as always to our anonymous benefactor, we are in his/her debt for the continued great releases.

CE_notes:
When Helen Sung played at Dizzy's Club on March 1, 2020, the pianist never imagined it would be a full year before she returned to the stage. Just ten days later, COVID-19 was declared a global pandemic. Music venues around the world closed doors and all tours were canceled or postponed indefinitely. Like musicians and artists everywhere, Sung turned to arts organizations for support and was fortunate enough to receive grants to continue creating music. 

In this concert filmed at Dizzy's on March 11, 2021 Helen Sung and her quartet play several pieces born out of the sorrow, loss, anxiety caused by the pandemic. There is no audience in attendance

thus, no applause. But between songs, she says, We hope to see you soon again, on stage, somewhere in person. 

That hope is starting to bear fruit. Sung recently recorded a double album with her quartet. Her collaboration with Miriam King, a dancer and neurorehabilitation researcher, was selected for the New Music USA 2021 Creator Development Fund. And recently, Sung was awarded a Guggenheim Fellowship. --NIKKI BIRCH--

Learn more about Helen Sung and her background in our radio episode:

FM radio broadcast by "Battiti dal Vivo", Radio3 RAI [third channell of Italian national radio], on sunday 10 October 2021, 24:07 hours [CET].
Il suono ricco e vibrante, la presenza ritmica solidissima e l'inesauribile vena melodica, sono tra le qualità più caratteristiche di Henri Texier (nella foto), colonna del jazz transalpino. Sin dagli anni '60 il suo contrabasso ha segnato la scena francese: dalle prime esperienze free, passando per il rock psichedelico, con il quartetto Transatlantik (con Joe Lovano, Steve Swallow e Aldo Romano), fino al progetto Carnet de Route (con Louis Sclavis e Aldo Romano) realizzato insieme al fotografo Guy Le Querrec. Questa notte ascoltiamo Henri Texier in concerto insieme al figlio Sébastien Texier al sax alto e al batterista Gautier Garrigue, un trio rodato con cui il contrabbassista ha già dato alle stampe diversi dischi. Il concerto in assenza di pubblico è stato registrato lo scorso febbraio da Radio France al Le Triton, un jazz club della banlieue parigina. Buon ascolto!
