This was recorded just a few rows back from the PA stack on the left side of the theater. My first concert and recording attempt since the pandemic began. Mentioning that by way of explaining a few very minor issues with the recording. The Edirol conked out due to me trying to monitor the fact that it was recording for no more than a few seconds at the end of tracks 2 and 3. Nothing was lost here of consequence beyond slight end of song flourishes and/or applause. The third time was a drop out of a few seconds towards the beginning of Zenith Blue. Other than these spots, it's a good audience capture. 
Just have to say that I'm not really knocked out by Side Eye. The players are great, but Pat seems to be turning a little bit into an oldies act over the last few years. It's almost as though he thinks his audience might desert him if he debuts or features "too much" new or current music. I don't see many jazz artists taking this tack in their performances, and I'm curious that he's doing this. I also wish there was a dedicated bassist. We all know the many fine bassists that he's employed over the years. I know Pat has said this is a nod back to his early days in a B3 Organ Trio, but it really isn't when considering the band's repertoire, and the array of keys that Francies uses. The "Jaco" sound on Bright Size Life is cool, but kind of canned.
Sorry for those asides. It is fabulous to hear musicians of this caliber live again. To mix musical genre references, Long May They Run. Please support them by paying to see them, and by purchasing their commercially released material.

Pat Metheny: From all of us, thank you very much. We're really kind of overwhelmed to be here and really excited. This is something we don't get the chance to do too often - play for
90. ,000 people or something, but I'm really, really happy that we could all be here. This band and me as a musician have a real loving relationship with Montreal and this festival in
particular, and to be here to celebrate 10 years is really something special for us, so it's a real treat and a real honor to be here tonight.

This was originally shared by Luckymusic as an NTSC DVD. The original lineage details about how this was transferred from VHS to DVD are lacking, but it seems to have been done very well
because there are no digital artifacts and the picture quality is quite sharp for a VHS. The original DVD included Are You Going With Me which was officially released as part of
Festival International de Jazz de MontrÃ(C)al: 20 Years of Music - 1980-2000 , so I had to remove it as well as the commercials from the broadcast.

I used XMedia Recode in copy mode to convert the DVD into a single .mp4 file. I then used Avidemux to split the video up into 6 individual .mkv segments that contained all the material
that I wanted to include. The final video was created by combining the individual .mkv segments using MKVToolNix GUI. There are no chapters. All these operations on the video were
lossless and did not require re-encoding, so the included content here looks and sounds identical to the original DVD.

Pedro Caldeira Cabral (Portugese guitar), Duncan Fox (double bass), Joaquim Silva (acoustic guitar). 

Pedro Caldeira Cabral (Lisbon, 1950) is an exceptional figure in today's music world. 
This outstanding performer plays a vast instrumental repertoire spanning the Mediaeval, Renaissance, Baroque, and Classic periods of Iberian Music, but also includes Portuguese traditional folk music influences, the 20th century repertoire of great Portuguese guitarists and his own compositions. 
Pedro Caldeira Cabral is undoubtedly a maestro of the Portuguese guitar. 
He is both composer and musician, playing professionally several string and wind instruments from different epochs since the age of sixteen. 
His main instrument is the Portuguese guitar (Citara Lusitanica) with which he has achieved a phenomenal level of mastery, 
expressiveness and virtuosity. 

With his 'Labyrinth of the Portuguese guitar', 
Pedro Caldeira Cabral lays the focus on making the biography of this marvelous and unique instrument audible. 
By accurately interpreting music of the last five centuries, 
Pedro Caldeira Cabral drives us through a most beautiful and very varied voyage in time and space.

Comments:
Lars Van de Voorde was first introduced to the piano at the age of 13 and was soon introduced to jazz music by his then teacher and mentor Werner Meert. He studied for two years with pianist Ron Van Rossum at the Lemmens Institute in Leuven and graduated from the Royal Conservatoire in Antwerp under Erik Vermeulen where he obtained his master's degree.
This is also where he got to know Jesse Dockx and Jef Manderveld, who now form the solid basis of his permanent trio. In the Lars Van de Voorde trio, improvisation and interaction are key, which makes each performance different and fresh. Jesse, Jef and Lars try to approach each performance with an open mind and without too many preconceived ideas.

Jesse Dockx started drumming at a young age and went to the Royal Conservatoire in Antwerp via StArt Muziek at Heilig Graf in Turnhout. This year, he is successfully completing his master's studies. To further develop himself as a musician, he will leave for New York next year.

He took lessons from Dré Pallemaerts, Mark Schilders, Stéphane Galland and Billy Hart, among others. Despite his young age, he is already playing at home and abroad and has released albums with projects such as Mamutrio & Anti-Panopticon. He has also played with Bert Joris, Tutu Puoane, the Brussels Jazz Orchestra, and others.

Jef Manderveld started playing the bass guitar at the age of fourteen, soon followed by the double bass. He continued his studies at the Kunsthumaniora van Antwerpen and went on to the conservatory, where he is now completing his master's degree. In the meantime, he has taken lessons from Piet Verbist, Nic Thys and Nathan Wouters, among others, and plays in various projects as a sideman.

https://www.chicagotribune.com/news/ct-xpm-1986-07-09-8602180672-story.html

WOODS KEEPS THE HEAT DOWN IN A COOL SET

Larry Kart, Entertainment writer

CHICAGO TRIBUNE July 9, 1986

For some time now--more than 25 years, in fact--I`ve felt that alto saxophonist Phil Woods has a problem, although Woods and his numerous admirers understandably don`t agree.

Briefly, the problem has to do with the way Woods tries to inject heat into his playing--as he puts a growling edge on his tone, indulges in steamy tremolos and proceeds to further agitate the rhythmic surface of his already quite syncopated lines.

I suppose that by saying ''tries to inject heat,'' I`m prejudging the matter

for Woods could reply that the devices that seem dubious to me are natural and deeply felt expressions of the man Woods is. But those traits certainly weren`t present in 1955, when Woods was an appealing newcomer

and their advent a few years later was, again in my opinion, not a welcome development.

None of this would matter if Woods were not a player of considerable talent: a technical master who has lots of agile harmonic and rhythmic ideas. But each time I hear him, much the same thing occurs.

An initial tune, which Woods May think of as a warm-up number, finds him playing in a relaxed, melodically fertile manner. Then the thermostat is turned way up, and the music begins to get--well, ''jazzy'' is the only word that comes to mind.

Tuesday night at the Jazz Showcase, though, the jazzy element was less apparent than usual

and Woods` first solo was an absolute gem: a series of light, joyfully dancing variations on composer Joe Roccisano`s elaborate anthology of bebop licks.

Appealing, too, was the seldom-heard ''Serenade in Blue,'' which featured a warm flugelhorn solo from Tom Harrell, and a medium-tempo Joe Emlee piece called ''Ya Know,'' which strode along with a poker-faced grace that recalled Horace Silver`s more harmonically adventurous work from the late 1950s.

All in all, it was one of the better Phil Woods sets I`ve heard in some time. And I`m sure that those who always have long been in Woods` corner felt it was much better than that.

PHIL WOODS QUINTET

Woods, alto saxophone

An open air concert in an amphiteater-like venue with again about 2500 attendence/sellout. Wonderful place to enjoy music.
This sunday evening was following a hot day, which resulted in that the audience was a little less focused, than the two days before.
We had 2 new couples in front and left next to us, that preferred to talk throughout the 2 concerts, than to listen to the wonderful music.
So if you hear during i.e. tune #7 a deep voice, it's that idiot right in front of us telling his wife/girlfriend very important stuff.
Sorry about that, but we couldn't do anything about it.
This band consisted of 4 wonderful musicians, that were able to create Chet Baker's music in a very traditional, but enjoyable way.
As we've never heard of this band or the musicians before, we were very positivly surprised.
The drummer might not have entirely the class of the other 3 musicians, but as an ensemble they presented the music very well.

I hope you enjoy the show as much as we did.

De Italiaanse trompettist Enrico Rava is de vader van de Italiaanse jazzscéne. Internationaal is hij ook de meest bekende jazzmuzikant, die meer dan honderd opnamen op zijn naam heeft, waarvan dertig als leider. Als trompettist is hij een bewonderaar van Miles Davis en Chet Baker (1929-1988), aan wie hij een hommage betuigt.

De Belgische gitarist Philip Catherine speelde in de jaren tachtig lange tijd aan de zijde van het Baker met bassist Jean-Louis Rassinfosse. Catherine is een gitarist in de lijn van Django Reinhardt. Hij kan zijn gitaar laten zingen, maar haalt er ook wondermooie loopjes uit en schuwt ook enig experiment of forse akkoorden niet. Maar hij is bovenal iemand die de melodie koestert en zich lyrisch kan uitleven. Met Chet Baker klikte het wonderwel.

Drummer Aldo Romano heeft Italiaanse wortels, maar verhuisde als kind al naar Frankrijk en verkoos in Parijs zijn geluk te zoeken. Hij is vandaag een van de elder statesman van de Franse jazzscéne. Met wie speelde hij niet Hij blijft steeds een gentleman, ook op het drumstel. Hij is een elegante, maar ook accurate en swingende drummer. Met Louis Sclavis en Henri Texier vormt hij een prachtig trio. De jongste jaren ontpopte hij zich ook als jazzzanger.

Ricardo Del Fra, ook al met Italiaanse wortels, is een rustige, maar zeer melodische bassist met een prachtige toon. In 1979 leert hij Chet Baker kennen. Hij bleef er negen jaar mee spelen en maakte er twaalf albums mee. Hij begreep Chet Baker en kon zich volkomen in diens muzikale wereld inleven. In 1989 maakte hij het album A Sip of your Touch, een anagram van A Touch of your Lips, dat Chet graag speelde. Hij noemt Chet een elegante meester van de muziek en de stilte.

Here's a very curious combination of great musicians in a set that doesn't seem to be too widely circulated. I got this many years ago in a cd-r trade with a trader from Euope (thanks to him), but I'm not sure if this has been here before on DIME. The connecting point here is Gurtu. He had recorded with Catherine on his End of August album in 1982, which also had included Charlie Mariano (for anyone who recently grabbed a Pork Pie or Catherine/Mariano/Van't Hof show here). By the time of this show Gurtu had been a member of Oregon with Towner for a few years, and was about to move on to his association with John McLaughlin.
I know nothing of the circumstances behind this show. Were they doing a series of shows, or was this a one off? No idea, but they seem to be enjoying themselves in each other's company from the between song commentary. It's a great artifact of the collaboration of these 3. Catherine soon turns 80. He just had a new recording released today in the US, and Towner is a little older, and I've just seen that he's got a new release upcoming soon on ECM. Trilok is still making music as well, and someone just shared a recent set he did with Jan Garbarek. The most recent recording I'm aware of him doing under his own name is a 2020 dics called God is a Drummer.
Thanks again to the trader who made this available to me, and to whoever it was that first recorded and shared this. Please do support these musicans by paying to see them live and by purchasing their commercially released materials.

This is a recording that comes from pretty early in the fine collaborations that these 2 musicians engaged in from the 70's through the 90's. They did the Sargasso Sea album on ECM the year of this performance, and there is one show of theirs from Frankfurt i September of 76 that was shared here about 5 years ago. It seems that this particular show might've been more a Towner gig because of the 2 solo openers by him, and the fact that you'll hear him bring on Abercrombie through a stage announcement.
I know nothing about the recording circumstances, but everything is clear enough that I've seen this listed as an FM, although I think it's probably a really excellent audience capture (given the 1976 recording date).
Thanks to the trader that made this available to me, and to whoever recorded and shared this to begin with.Please support all of the musicians you admire by purchasing their commercially released material, and through paying to see them live when possible.

Just happened to listen to the ECM duo album these 2 did in the late 90's called A Closer View a few days aga, and was struck by how fine of a pairing they made. That got me looking at what shows I might have from them. This earlier NDR Funkhaus capture nearer to the time of their Oracle album seemed like a good one to bring back. It's been some time since it appeared here. There's a nice Austrian show from 2000 that's still active, but this one hasn't seemed to be up since 2007 when I grabbed it as it was shared by jmgdiscs. It had been up once before in 2005 from rommedoe with the idea that it somehow connected to Rudolff (no surprise there). I'm including a bit from the earlier notes and the source info copied from the dimebot archive below.
The samples will show how fine of a recording this is, and nothing new seemed to be needed relative to the files, other than renaming track 3 from Waltz for Debby to My Romance and ID'ing the previously unknown Track 12 as Nardis. I'm including the Unknown tracks in samples so someone might hopefully be able to ID them. 2 of these find Ralph on piano, which he didn't play on either of the duo albums, and the fact that he does here is a nice addition to the tonal pallette. Each of these tracks sounds like a standard to me, or something possibly done by Bill Evans, but I may be wrong there. If anyone does have titles, please write them below in the comments. Huge thanks to those who've made this available to the rest of us.

This audience recording should not to be confused with the NPR Jazz Alive broadcast of parts of the previous day's performance by this trio at this venue.

The late and much missed MM recorded this show from the audience using an unknown stereo cassette recorder. A copy of his now-lost master was made using a conventional bias BASF tape not long after the show. That copy was digitized in 2020 using a JVC KD-D55 cassette deck via Goldwave. For some reason, the volume of the music on the left channel of the cassette drops significantly near the end of the first side and is similarly weaker and hissier on the entire second side of the cassette. To address this problem when the recording was digitized, the much stronger right channel was copied and pasted over the weaker left channel at these points via Goldwave. The abrupt change from ambient stereo to true mono is noticeable. Goldwave was also used to boost the overall volume of the recording and for minor edits.

)

This my friends is a true GEM in every sense of the word.

This performance was recorded off the air in the early 1980s from a Washington DC-area FM station (WETA WPFW) that was carrying the American Jazz Radio Theatre, which sometimes re-broadcast WBGO broadcasts from the Village Vanguard, and which appeared to be an attempt to fill the void left when NPR ceased producing Jazz Alive! . It is not from the three Red Rodney-Ira Sullivan official releases that were recorded at the Village Vanguard in 1980. Those releases had a different bassist and drummer, according to the information found at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Ira_Sullivan_live_albums and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Red_Rodney_live_albums.

The date of this performance is uncertain. Unlike the announcers for Jazz Alive! broadcasts, the announcers for these re-broadcasts rarely if ever gave the dates of the performances. However, some evidence suggests that it took place in 1982. On track 02, Sullivan refers to an album he and Rodney had recently made for Elektra Musician -- apparently the 1981 LP Spirit Within (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spirit_Within). Also, Anderson and Hirshfield appeared on a live LP that the group recorded at a different venue in November 1982 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sprint_(album)). Finally, a June 1, 1982 New York Times article refers to the Rodney-Sullivan group's upcoming appearance at the Village Vanguard (https://www.nytimes.com/1982/06/01/arts/going-out-guide.html), although it also refers to them playing there often.

That said, there is no reference to a post-1980 live recording by this line-up at the Vanguard in these listings of official releases by Red Rodney and/or Ira Sullivan.

comments:
This is the earliest full length RTF show I've ever heard, sort of a bridge
between the acoustic jazz Chick of before, and what would follow. For most of his long musical life, Corea has played with great guitarists, such as George Benson and then John McLaughlin, before this, Connors and DiMeola after. This concert features songs of the 1st 2 RTF albums, (both studio, not this studio, and now available on CD.) Return to Forever and Light as a Feather , probably the jazziest RTF of all. Stanley Clarke also had a solo studio album called Children of Forever which had a similar lineup and style of music as the 1st 2 RTF albums. All 3 of those are nice listening. There May be a song from that in here too. If you like RTF but don't like fusion , this is your RTF torrent. (there are some RTF fans like that, especially for this stuff, which sounds very different than anything after 72), it's jazz. Not jazz rock fusion . I think this May sound a little better than my recent 75 RTF Gothenburg post, which came from the same reliable source as this one, Chris in Germany. (thank you very much
for sharing this Chickness). it's from a clean low-gen. FM tape, the end of matrix fades out early but the rest seems to be complete. I think that fadeout May be in the broadcast which was pre-recorded. This recording includes several songs not heard in any of my other RTF posts, and is the only good recording of this band I have. Based on the length of it I doubt there's much missing, but as we've heard especially in 2 Worcester 74 shows (w/Connors) Chick has always liked playing long songs. (playing with Miles Davis will develop that habit quick) He's got plenty to choose from, even this early on, and these are mostly ones you aren't likely to hear (except Maybe Spain) if you're going to a 2008 show. Like the two that followed, this was also a superior quality lineup, Maybe the first chance for many to hear the playing of Farrell, Stanley Clarke, or Airto, who all have since done very well during and after being Chicked . This was not Corea's 1st time being a bandleader, however, and more about that later. This is, I believe his first go round doing it with the group Corea is probably now most familiar from (other than Miles Davis in 69-70, it don't get ANY bigger than that in jazz music). As I think you'll find out, there is no such thing as any less than a very good RTF song, at this early point. Filling up a 2 hour+ concert with solid songs wasn't a problem at all even on their 1st world tour.

I first saw RTF on a double bill with Larry Coryell and Offering at a small club in Greenwich Village when I was 16 or 17. Those were heady times with other firsts like seeing Mahavishnu and Weather Report, while also rushing off to see Yes, King Crimson, or Gentle Giant. Definitely game changers for me and many others back then. 
I was checking any good sounding shows I had from that period for possible re-seeds when I came across this. It sparked my interest right away because Daryll Brown was drumming. He was in RTF? He sure was. Very interesting in that he also played with Weather Report live, but he never went into the studio with either band. He does a fine job here as he shares percussion duties with Mingo Lewis. Not sure how or why he came and went from RTF. The earlh gig I saw myself had Steve Gadd drumming, and of course there originally had been Airto, and later Lenny White. The added plus with any RTF from this era is Bill Connors, who I always liked more than the celebrated Mr. Dimeola. The Vulcan Worlds, Pharoah Kings, No Mystery's, and Romantic Warriors all were to come, and to great acclaim, but there was something about Connor's string bending and phase shifter that always resonated with me-along with the material from Hymn of the Seventh Galaxy. Another interesting thing about this show is that the band is still featuring things from the Airto/Flora/Joe Farrell RTF. You'll actually here Chick say that this gig has them playing Hymn of the Seventh Galaxy for the very first time.
You'll see below a reference to a version of this that michaelmee and Fekete had shared, but this seemingly more complete one came from mr. mags and agalli. Thanks to the mr. mags/agalli combo for all of the fine shows they've brought our way. Here's the original info file:

This is a torrent I need to upload because it is probably the best recording there is of this show, and there was an incomplete version of this posted several months ago on dime. This is complete and all of it comes from cassettes made from the original radio master reel. This is not an FM broadcast version, but as some call it, a pre-FM . I simply call it a soundboard. I worked at WCUW radio from 1987-2001, and hosted a show there for over 10. years that featured recorded live in concert recordings, about 200 of which were my own. Most were bands few have likely heard of, but a few are definitely worth hearing and will be heard in time, along with several from my own archives. This was about 14 years before I was at WCUW, and one of WCUW's first concert broadcast recordings, in the original tape (some too on this but a little less so) I could hear parts where all of a sudden the drums would get loud and the bass and guitar go way in the background. RTF is probably a tough band to mix sound for, because they like to feature all their players at various times (as in this most interesting pair of shows.) so there's a tendency to turn up one guy and then turn him down after the solo. It takes a real pro sound(wo)man to do that right at a RTF concert, and this person seemed to have some trouble at times with it. But after some level adjusting in needed places I'm finally not only content, but anxious to upload this torrent because it sounds pretty nice now. When I first got it I didn't know jack about computers, never mind torrents. I got this in a snail trade many years ago from a fellow in Ohio. The recording is pretty good, the mix is a little off in parts, a little distorted in parts, pretty clear in most parts. (Alot of these RTF college gigs have strange mixing, see my Worcester 2/1/74 show for more evidence of that) White and Corea come through clearly throughout, Clarke and DiMeola's mix varies a little more. Track 7 is about 48 minutes long. This is one of the longer RTF shows
I've heard with Al DiMeola. It is a very good performance. Vulcan Worlds is 22 minutes +. The only tape flip interruption comes just after the acoustic jam, just before theme to the mothership starts the first group segment. You May not even notice the splice. Beyond the 7th galaxy is only about 3 min. (this is not very
unusual) all the other songs are much longer. It sounds like this recording comes from an all normal bias/eq setting tape lineage. (this does tend to help preserve the clarity of a normal-bias/EQ recording, which all analog tapes were until high bias tape came out circa later 70's, whereas an all high-bias tape lineage helps to
keep tape noise down and bass response good.)

comments:
I got this on a reel from a guy who had it on a reel... there May be a third reel in the lineage of this but I'm certain that no cassettes and no dolby was used on any of them. It sounds like the whole show (unless after half an hour of solos and a 25 minute Celebration Suite, they had enough gas left in the tank for an encore) although all the talking by Chick and the band was edited out on the copy I recieved. Disc 1 ends with a 25 minute (standard
length) Song to the Pharoah Kings, one of my favorite live RTF songs. The quality on this is pretty nice, not quite pristine, doesn't sound generated and a decent mix of the instruments (some a little off, but not as much as in the Clark Univ. w/Connors show of Feb. 1, 74). It's got plenty of energy. It was impossible to avoid a cut on this master, even on a reel unless somebody had the foresight to know after the Pharoah Kings (about an hour into show)
would be the last break with enough time to flip a reel over- unless they were using a two-directional reel machine (those come in very handy at RTF concerts), but whoever recorded this managed to cut twice, once near end of Corea's piano solo, and again near the end of Lenny White's solo, just before they go into the Celebration Suite. (This would seem to be the logical place to flip it over, if the recording person did not know the setlist before the show.) Not much is missing, the rest of the music appears to be all here, nice
to hear Pharoah and Celebration in the same show (and both uninterrupted) Good ones too, those are my favorite parts of this show. I'd be quite surprised if any copy of this sounds noticably better than this. I think all the reels in this lineage were/are Maxells recorded at 3 3/4 ips.

Ricola Notes:
Another broken Reel to Reel tape which I repaired and just finished to transfer on CD.

Editing Notes:
-Original audio had a significant phase error with the left channel leading the right by on average 17 samples, 
 with some variation
-Automatic phase corrections to handle the variations
-Levels started off reasonably balanced, but the right channel became significantly weaker as the recording progressed
-Constant amplification of 3 dB to the left channel, and automatic, varying level adjustments to the right channel to 
 balance with the left

-Original audio was running considerably slow - almost a whole tone, 11.5%, but at least it was consistently off
-Because it was running so slow, the more appropriate new sampling frequency is actually 48 kHz instead of 44.1 kHz in order to preserve more of the information that Ricola captured in the original transfer (not that there's actually very useful detail in those high frequencies here - it's just tape hiss > 10 kHz)
-So instead of resampling (speed adjusting) by 11.5% to correspond to a 44.1 kHz sampling frequency, the resampling 
 factor was only 1.115*44.1/48 = 1.0244 or 2.44%
-All edits done in MATLAB
-ledwhofloyd (Ross), Jan. 2023

Not only was RTF playing fusion music but their concerts were usually fusions. In this case, the opener was the rock group Orleans (inc. future NY Congressman John Hall). The next year saw Renaissance opening
for RTF. Today only festival crowds would quietly sit through such contrasting styles. Enjoy! Thanks to RTF for a lot of great music and for last year's reunion!

This is a new take on a fine audience capture from the RTF European tour that promoted the most popular verion of the band's final work together, Romantic Warrior. This was originally shared by mr. mags in 2011, so big thanks to him and to whoever he'd gotten it from-along with the person who recorded and began circulating the show. Ian (glasnostrd19) did a reworking of it almost immediately after that to deal with some tracking issues and a few dead spots within those tracks. It doesn't appear to have been up here since that version fell off the tracker in 2012.
I've now taken on another reworking that was motivated by rediscovering my copy of mr.mags' 2011 share on disc, being impressed by what I heard, and realizing there were some things I knew how to do through audio editing that I felt might enhance it further. I'd never gotten Ian's reworking of this show, I don't think he did any actual sonic changes to the music from the 2011 share. I did see what he had done thanks to the dimebot archive, and I did do a few of the same types of things he had done relative to splicing a few dead spots, and making sure that tracks started with music rather than applause, as they often did in the mr. mags share. Along those lines, I created a separate track for Lenny White's spoken intro to Romantic Warrior and the acoustic music that followed. Not sure about this, but a tape cut right before that might've indicated some sort of break or short intermission before this part of the show. I did see them near to this time, but don't recall if that type of break in the show was done or not. Finally, there was a very short separate track of applause and a brief stage announcement before Space Circus, which I spliced on to the applause at the end of track 11.
I did all of my editing and re-tracking work on the files in Audacity. Most notably, I've also utilized a couple of their VST MuseFX plugins Simple EQ (the "Presence" preset at level 5 out of 11), and Mastering (the "More Exciting" preset at level 3.5 out of 11). I'm sure some may want to crucify me for that, but rather than immediately doing so, please listen to the samples to see if you find them to have improved the quality of the music (I do), and/or simply choose to bypass this share. There are also a few professionally recorded shows from RTF near to this time that do circulate (11/75 Hempstead, NY

and the OGWT from the UK), so they will all be superior to this share. That said, this was a pretty remarkable audience capture to begin with, and I believe it to be even better in this form. You'll be able to judge for yourself from the samples below. They include the music as it was in the 2011 share followed by how the same basic spot will now sound thanks to the Audacity tweaks.
I'm lucky enough to have seen RTF a few times back to right before Hymn of the Seventh Galaxy when Steve Gadd was briefly on drums, and Bill Connors was on guitar. I loved Hymn and the first post-Connors album, Where Have I Known You Before, but found less to like on either No Mystery or Romantic Warrior. Music Magic would take the band to different places beyond any of this, and soon Chick would abandon the band name altogether for a while. This show isn't from my particular sweet spot with RTF, and I know others have different opinions as to when that might've been. In any case, this is a fine document of the band at what certainly was their commercial peak, and a time when the notes were flying fast and furiously from all four of the members.

comments:
there were some rather loud mike knocks, mostly between songs which have been reduced to make them less intrusive to this Romantic Warrior tour concert. this recording seems to be missing part of the beginning, since the second part of the concert begins with track 3 here. presumably the first part was about 45 minutes, as was usual for this magnificent tour.
only the first 3 tracks are romantic warrior songs. on this tour they usually also played Sorceress (by Lenny White, heard on this RTF album, and also in some of Lenny's solo shows)
and another song or two from the Romantic Warrior album
(either the Magician, and/or Majestic Dance) so this is probably missing at least one or two songs of the beginning of the show. Medevial Overture cuts in slightly, but seems to have everything after that. the last 2 songs are not usual RTF songs played (solo Al tunes, usually) but the recording and audience quality sounds similar enough that it is probably from the same concert. they usually did play at least one encore song on this tour, if time allowed, if not 2 fairly short ones
Celebration Suite is usually a long one, but sometimes (including this show), they just played the short ending part of it to wind up another song, as they did here with Lopsy Lu, from one of Stanley's early solo albums.

comments:
this show was previously posted with severe glitching in a few of the tracks, and when I heard that I asked mr mags if he could get another copy of the recording, because it's a Romantic Warrior concert, and aside from a few rather minor flaws in the source recording, it's a pretty enjoyable recording. He followed up on that request and sent me this, which has no glitches at all. there are some edits between songs, apparently in the source recording. I would guess this is the whole show.
not sure if there was a set break (as there was at Boston Nov. 75 world premiere of the music in this tour). if so the second set likely began with Romantic Warrior, or they May have begun it after that. I think it begins with RW because there's
some talk and tuning before it, and there's no edit after that, there's applause and it goes into the piano solo after that. Otherwise I would have put the RW with disc 1. that's a better time balance of discs, but I think it's a 2 set show with an intermission after track 5. that's why I split it this uneven way.
some music I can take or leave, some I like and a few pieces of music grab me like a 500 pound lineman. My jaw was last seen at the Orpheum Theater (after it fell off) after the Romantic Warrior concert there. this was an experience I will never forget. one can't expect that Boston night of pure magic
to be repeated in a fieldhouse in Iowa, although alot of folks were quite unprepared for what hit them. this was one of the finest fusion tours by anybody, in the opinion of some, the pinnacle year for RTF, much like 1973 was with the
Mahavishnu Orchestra.

An outstanding performance !!

There were a number of tech problems including Al's amp
and monitor levels. Right through to the encore,
the band was regularly signalling to the crew or
they were on-stage. Al was particularly frustrated
during Song to the Pharoah Kings. I wonder how much
these distractions affected the soloing - I couldn't tell.

With this recording, the sonic levels vary tremendously.
As a result, despite the taper being 20 feet in front
of the left stacks, the levels are low on the
acoustic sections. The levels could have been
adjusted via remastering but then it would hide
the incredible range through which RTF took the audience.

Having taped the band in March 1975 and promoted
a sold-out Renaissance-RTF show in 1976, this was
a nostalgic and wonderful night of music.

+media.CE_notes:
This wonderful recording was taken directly from the live broadcast on the night and included radio talk before and after the broadcast as well as talking over most of the band's between-tune comments (especially Chick's and Stanley's). I have edited those radio comments out as much as possible (as I don't like the flow of the show to be interrupted by radio announcers), which means Chick's and Stanley's banter has been lost although Jean-Luc's has been saved. There were a few FM pops, which I have edited out as well and I have cleaned up two breaks in the broadcast. There is an FM signal at 19000 Hz, but I didn't find it distracting. The first part of the broadcast is in mono, at about 2:07 into t02 the signal changes to stereo.

This is a wonderful show, probably only missing Spain and a School Days encore (which was played regularly as an encore on this tour).

notes from orchiddoctor
What can I say about Roscoe Mitchell In my opinion, he is the king of them all. Certainly in the late 70s, he was the most sought out musician in the bunch. Besides seeing in with the AEC some 30 times, I saw him at the Wildflowers festival, with Muhal (and Air), in  Septet, in a trio with Oliver Lake and Philip Wilson, and solo. All but the Wildflowers (available commercially) is going up on Dime. I have many memories of Roscoe. Sometimes he would just show up to hear someone else play and then hang out. Often, we would catch a set at the Palace and then walk over to the West Side to catch a set of someone else. I walked with Muhal several times and once with Scowie. We talked about his disdain for the fact that his music (and others') was drawing a predominately white audience with few blacks in attendance, We agreed that the white audience heard things in a more cerebral manner while black folks heard the ancestral rhythms.
At any rate, he was pleased that so many people were opening up their ears, minds and hearts to listen to this music. If you're reading this, you already have. Enjoy!

It's been 9 long years since Scott's last stop in Chicago (also at Martyrs'), and surely worth the wait! It was a very entertaining night full of laughter and great fusion. The guys seemed very loose and relaxed, considering the fact that they were stuck in Indianapolis on their way to Chicago, due to a busted fuel pump in their van, arriving only 15 minutes prior to the start of their set. This was the final night of the US tour, and to top it off this recording turned out EXCELLENT. It captures the vibe of the night to a tee. I am extremely happy with the final result. Hope you enjoy this fantastic long, single set. 

And last, but not least: RICO!!! This one's for you, my fine friend:)

Relocating and transferring this VHS tape has taken the better part of the last few weeks. This 50 minute documentary, filmed by Canadian Public Broadcasting, is filled with spiritual wisdom and live performances as the band practices and performs during a tour of Europe. In case you haven't heard their music, it's sort of a cross between Ravi Shankar (in fact that's his son in the band) and fast, uplifting jazz. One of the locations filmed during the day is a concert in a bullfighting ring in the Provence section of France. McLaughlin's playing is *incredible*.

A couple of technical notes: There are a few, very small dropouts that were present during the transfer. One of them occured right at the end of the credits, so the transfer was ended just before the video dropped.

Sonny Sharrock
From Wikipedia
> 2022-03-29

Warren Harding "Sonny" Sharrock (August 27, 1940 ' May 25, 1994)[1] was an American jazz guitarist. He was married to singer Linda Sharrock, with whom he recorded and performed. One of few guitarists in the first wave of free jazz in the 1960s, Sharrock was known for his heavily chorded attack, his highly amplified bursts of feedback, and his use of saxophone-like lines played loudly on guitar. He wanted to play tenor saxophone from his youth after hearing John Coltrane on Davis's Kind of Blue on the radio at age 19, but his asthma prevented this. Sharrock said repeatedly, however, that he still considered himself "a horn player with a really fucked up axe."

Early life and career

He was born in Ossining, New York, United States.[1] Sharrock began his musical career singing doo wop in his teen years.[1] He collaborated with Pharoah Sanders and Alexander Solla in the late 1960s, appearing first on Sanders's 1966 album, Tauhid.[1] He made several appearances with flautist Herbie Mann,[1] and an uncredited appearance on Miles Davis's A Tribute to Jack Johnson.

Career revival

After the release of Paradise, Sharrock was semi-retired for much of the 1970s, undergoing a divorce from his wife and occasional collaborator Linda in 1978. In the intermittent years until bassist Bill Laswell coaxed him out of retirement, he worked as both a chauffeur and a caretaker for mentally challenged children. At Laswell's urging, Sharrock appeared on Material's (one of Laswell's many projects) 1981 album, Memory Serves. In addition, Sharrock was a member of the punk/jazz band Last Exit, with Peter BrÃ¶tzmann, Laswell and Ronald Shannon Jackson. During the late 1980s, he recorded and performed extensively with the New York-based improvising band Machine Gun, as well as leading his own bands. Sharrock flourished with Laswell's help, noting in a 1991 interview that "the last five years have been pretty strange for me, because I went twelve years without making a record at all, and then in the last five years, I've made seven records under my own name. That's pretty strange."

Laswell would often perform with the guitarist on his albums, and produced many of Sharrock's recordings, including the entirely solo Guitar, the metal-influenced Seize the Rainbow, followed by one of his more universally accessible albums, High Life. Sonny was quoted as saying that this was his favorite band ever, with Abe Speller on drums, Lance Carter on drums, Charles Baldwin on bass and David Snider on keyboards. This was followed by the well-received Ask the Ages, which featured John Coltrane's bandmates Pharoah Sanders and Elvin Jones. "Who Does She Hope To Be?" is a lyrical piece harkening back to the Coltrane/Davis Kind of Blue sessions that had inspired him to play. One writer described Ask the Ages as "hands down, Sharrock's finest hour, and the ideal album to play for those who claim to hate jazz guitar."

Death and Tributes

On May 26, 1994, Sharrock died of a heart attack in his hometown of Ossining, New York, on the verge of signing the first major label deal of his career. He was 53. French guitarist NoÃ«l AkchotÃ(C)'s 2004 album Sonny II features tracks written, performed and inspired by Sharrock.
Sharrock is also known for the soundtrack to the Cartoon Network program Space Ghost Coast to Coast with his drummer Lance Carter, one of the last projects he completed in the studio before his death. The season 3 episode "Sharrock" carried a dedication to him at the end, and previously unheard music that he had recorded for the show featured throughout most of the episode. "Sharrock" premiered as the 23rd episode on March 1, 1996 on Cartoon Network.

Watch Sons of Kemet Recorded Live at Big Ears Festival 

 Jazz built for arenas. A friend and former rock critic shared this admiring assessment of Sons of Kemet, after seeing the band for the first time at this year's Big Ears Festival. There's obviously truth in it: Over the last eight years, Sons of Kemet has not only fueled the fires of a raging London jazz scene

it has also scaled up the pyrotechnics, in strictly musical terms.

With Shabaka Hutchings on tenor saxophone, Theon Cross on tuba, and Nache Edward and Tom Skinner on drums, it's a hardy combustion engine that also feels like a breathing organism. Arenas, sure, but this is also jazz built for street parties. And certain proudly eclectic fests.

At Big Ears in Knoxville, Tenn., Sons of Kemet brought its exultant blend of carnival rhythm, club abandon and jazz improv to a midnight show that packed The Mill & Mine, a cavernous room that once housed the Industrial Belting and Supply Company. The set drew from a knockout recent album, Your Queen Is a Reptile, but with a spirit of freedom in the moment - whatever setting you think suits it best, it's music made for a perpetual now. -- NATE CHINEN

Introduction to the Lost and Found Mike the MICrophone Series

Welcome to JEMS' Lost and Found Mike the MICrophone series presenting recordings made by legendary taper Mike Millard, AKA Mike The Mike, best known for his masters of Led Zeppelin done in and around Los Angeles circa 1975-77. For the complete details on how tapes in this series came to be lost and found again, as well as JEMS' long history with Mike Millard, please refer to the notes in Vol. One: http://www.dimeadozen.org/torrents-details.php?id=500680.

Until 2020, the Lost and Found series presented fresh transfers of previously unavailable first-generation copies made by Mike himself for friends like Stan Gutoski of JEMS, Jim R, Bill C. and Barry G. These sources were upgrades to circulating copies and in most instances marked the only time verified first generation Millard sources had been directly digitized in the torrent era.

That all changed with the discovery of many of Mike Millard's original master tapes.

Yes, you read that correctly, Mike Millard's master cassettes, long rumored to be destroyed or lost, have been found. Not all of them but many, and with them a much more complete picture has emerged of what Millard recorded between his first show in late 1973 and his last in early 1993.

The reason the rediscovery of his master tapes is such a revelation is that we've been told for decades they were gone. Internet myths suggest Millard destroyed his master tapes before taking his own life, an imprudent detail likely concocted based on the assumption that because his master tapes never surfaced and Mike's mental state was troubled he would do something rash WITH HIS LIFE'S WORK. There's also a version of the story where Mike's family dumps the tapes after he dies. Why would they do that?

The truth is Mike's masters remained in his bedroom for many years after his death in 1994. We know at least a few of Millard's friends and acquaintances contacted his mother Lia inquiring about the tapes at the time to no avail. But in the early 2000s, longtime Millard friend Rob S was the one she knew and trusted enough to preserve Mike's work.

The full back story on how Mike's master tapes were saved can be found in the notes for Vol. 18 Pink Floyd, which was the first release in our series transferred from Millard's original master tapes:

http://www.dimeadozen.org/torrents-details.php?id=667745&hit=1
http://www.dimeadozen.org/torrents-details.php?id=667750&hit=1

Stanley Clarke, Greek Theatre, Los Angeles, CA September 11, 1979

One of the revelations brought on by the discovery of previously uncirculated and uncredited Mike "The Mike" Millard recordings is the breadth of artists Mike captured. We add another great one to the list with this outstanding capture of the incredible bass player Stanley Clarke performing at the Greek in 1979.

Clarke was not only a leading light on the jazz-fusion (or more accurately jazz-funk) scene, but moved seemlessly between genres, seemingly just as comfortable touring with Chick Corea as with the Rolling Stones offshoot the New Barbarians.

Mike ended up see Clarke playing with both acts, as well as multiple times as a solo artist. This 1979 set sees him on tour in support of the double album I Wanna Play For You, songs from which are featured in the 11-song set along with covers of work by Charles Mingus and Charlie Parker.

That Clarke was playing a big venue like the Greek reflects how popular jazz and its rock and R&B flavored offshoots were at the time. Shame things aren't like that any more. Also check out the players in Clarke's band, aces all around. The playing here is outstanding and I find Clarke's lead bass work captivating.

As for Mike, the sound at smaller outdoor venues already works in one's favor and he makes an excellent pull this night, with wide fidelity from the bass to cymbals. Samples provided.

Here's what Jim R had to say about seeing Stanley Clarke and band at the Greek in 1979.

I went with Mike Millard to the Stanley Clarke concert at the Greek Theatre on Sept 11, 1979. We sat in Section A, Row G. This is seven rows behind the pit, dead center. We were elevated a bit above the stage. Great sight lines and definitely in our much desired "Sweet Spot."

The Greek Theatre is located inside Griffith Park near the famous observatory featured in Rebel Without a Cause. The setting is excellent for concerts--open air, offering a gentle, cooling breeze on a warm, late-summer evening and also great acoustics. Though it holds close to 6000 people, The Greek feels relatively intimate, making it one of the most desirable venues in SoCal. As a matter of fact, three days later Mike and I saw Joni Mitchell (Vol. 79 in the Lost and Found series). The venue had a strict "No Camera" policy so I left my camera bag at home for Stanley.

Mike and I loved seeing Clarke in concert. Just four months earlier in May, we saw him at the Forum as the bass player in the New Barbarians with Keith Richards and Ronnie Wood. We also saw Stanley several times at The Roxy in Hollywood. With his long, powerful fingers, Clarke could do things to a bass guitar few others could match. He is a wizard with a bass in his hands.

Stanley brought together an extremely gifted group of musicians, too. All of this easily won over a group of rowdy fans around us.

That's all I got for this one. I hope you enjoy the show as much as Mike and I did.

Cheers to my buddy Mike. RIP.

###

JEMS is proud to partner with Rob, Jim R, Ed F, Barry G, Jim Ri and many others to release Millard's historic recordings and to help set the record straight about the man himself.

We can't thank Rob enough for reconnecting with Jim and putting his trust in our Millard reissue campaign. He kept Mike's precious tapes under wraps for two decades, but once Rob learned of our methods and stewardship, he agreed to contribute the Millard DATs and cassettes to the program. Our releases would not be nearly as compelling without Jim's memories, photos and other background contributions. As many of you have noted, the stories offer an entertaining complement to Mike's incredible audio documents.

Another week, another thank you to those who make our weekly releases in the Lost and Found series possible. Professor Goody is always available to consult on pitch adjustments and each week's release is the better for it. Goody also helps with some of the more challenging setlists including this one. JEMS' own mjk5510 continues to manage our release queue and handle post production and artwork. We thank them both. Shout out to Rob as well for the tape transfer and to Jim R for finding his ticket stub.

Finally, here's to the late, great Mike the MICrophone. His work never ceases to impress. May he rest in peace.

BK for JEMS

Welcome to Volume 13 of our master series featuring the master recordings of dime member "tapetyrant". The series will predominately feature captures in the Northeast and Southern California areas. We will touch on multiple genres with a strong focus on Jazz Fusion, New Wave and Rock.

Tapetyrant was an active taper in the 1980's and much of the 1990's before, like many of us, hanging up the mics. What he captured during that time is uniformly excellent quality and his master tapes have been safely stored, the first batch are in pristine condition. Some shows May circulate from lower generation copies but most have remained uncirculated until now and have never circulated directly from the masters.

Prior to DAT, the heavy lifting was entirely done by a Sony D5 with NAK 300's and taping was serious business, acquiring the best seats possible and working to keep neighbors in check.

We move back into Jazz Fusion-Funk territory with another excellent TapeTyrant capture. Volume 13 features Stanley Clarke' September 11, 1984 performance at the Paradise Theater in Boston.

Stanley appears to stay away from the new release, 1984's "Time Exposure" released on August 28th to focus on past titles, highlighted with an electrifying version of 1976's "School Days".

For the encore Stanley has some fun saying "I'm finished with all the serious stuff and what I was hoping that there's some musicians or vocalists in the audience that want to come up and play with us", he proceeds to invite audience members who want to play or sing on stage for a 15 minute jam with the band making for a very cool and unique portion of the show.

Extra thanks this week to goody for doing double duty not only ensuring we're running at the proper pitch but pulling together the setlist for us.

Of course continued thanks to "tapetyrant" for doing such a great job capturing these important shows, for reaching out and entrusting me to present his excellent work for all to enjoy for decades to come.

We are indebted to his generosity (tapers don't let those tapes and your hard work get lost to the ages, there are plenty of folks to get in touch with here to help get them out, we're all working to leave no tape behind).

Artwork and samples included.

The Prince Bandroom is a venue I think is very sub-standard. It is a concrete bunker (including a pillar centre to stage one metre into the audience) painted black with a strong smell of stale beer (smoking now banned!). This gig was hardly advertised ( I found out because a friend saw a poster), which may account for only about 200 people in attendance. 

I have listened to Stanley Clarke over the years. I have a few vinyl and CDs. But I'm not an aficionado. Similarly, I'm very familiar with George Duke during his FZ years and have vinyl with Billy Cobham and some CDs. I am not going to research names for the nine tracks. I haven't got the time. I'm sure someone out there will do this with much less effort than I would need.

The sound level at the venue was very high. I had the lowest recording level selected, but there were still a few instances of 'clipping'. However, these are hardly noticeable. The balance has the drums and bass very strong with the keyboards lower than ideal. It is a clear and dynamic recording.

The original DVD had letterboxing problems - it was encoded at a 4:3 aspect ratio but the picture is actually 5:3 so there are significant black bars at the top and bottom. I used MakeMKV
to convert the DVD to mkv. To completely fix the letterboxing the video would have had to be re-encoded, but that would have slightly reduced the quality so I did not. Instead, I worked 
around the issue by using MKVToolNix to adjust the header information. I changed the display aspect ratio to 5:3 and cropped the default display area with the following parameters: 
Left 0, Top 60, Right 8, Bottom 62.

However, many media players (including VLC) do not recognize the header changes. One player that does is MPC-BE. With VLC, for example, to get the video to fill the screen you will have 
to manually change the display aspect ratio back to 4:3. Then go to Tools > Effects and Filters > Video Effects > Crop > Enter approximately the numbers I've given above.

Here's some wonderful acoustic music from this year's Jazz Fest - I had a great seat, there was very little audience chatter, except for two women in the row ahead of me during track 13, and the PA sounded quite good for the show being in a huge tent!

If you're familiar with the late, great gypsy guitarist Django Reinhardt, then you've probably heard of Stephane Wrembel...if not, you'll be amazed and quite possibly you'll chuckle aloud when you listen to this, thinking  how did he play that so fast  His bandmates aren't slouches either - the percussion, bass and rhythm guitar all mesh perfectly with Stephane's joyous fretwork :)

Sun Ra & His Arkestra: Rehearsal, Oakland, CA circa. October, 1971 (CDR)
In preparation for the Arkestra's second European tour scheduled to begin in October, 1971, Tommy 'Bugs' Hunter recorded this sixty-minute rehearsal segment sometime in lat September or early October -- or possibly a mere days before departure (see Campbell & Trent, p.173). This tape was subsequently broadcast by WKCR-FM during their Sun Ra memorial event on May 22, 1995 and now circulates widely amongst collectors. The rather crude monophonic recording offers a window into the inner workings of the core Arkestra as Sun Ra pontificates on various subjects and works the band through a handful of compositions, three of which were never performed again. This was apparently common practice, where numerous compositions were vigorously rehearsed, but never performed (see e.g., Id. p.170).
The tape opens with Ra talking about new experimental synthesizers and a 'secret' electronic instrument (sort of like a Theremin) which won't respond to a black person's skin. Of course, Sonny is bemused by the apparent racism of this 'mean' technology and chortles: 'You go talking about equal rights and here you got an instrument that won't play for you if you're black!' Even so, Ra is interested in the instrument's ability to play a 'purple C' and a 'red C' and play 'sixteen pitches between C and C#.' I have no idea what he's talking about, but he sure sounds convincing. Getting down to business, he leads the 10-member Arkestra through part of an unidentified title that sounds somewhat similar to the 'Discipline' series, with lushly harmonized horns playing slowly interweaving parts over a repeating bass ostinato. After a couple of minutes, Ra cuts things off to enquire whether James Jacson has been reached on the telephone in New Jersey regarding travel arrangements to Europe. (He wasn't home. 'He wasn't home last night, either,' Ra complains.) A lackadaisical run through of 'Love in Outer Space' follows which prompts Sonny to chide the drummers and wax enthusiastically about Clifford Jarvis, who was apparently eager to get his old job back. Even so, Sonny does acknowledge Jarvis's propensity to overplay: 'You can't just get a recording with nothing but drums, drums, drums, drums, drums. That's what I used to try to tell
> 127
Clifford Jarvis. Now, he took about a forty-minute solo on the thing'¦I told him, 'we're recording!' Made no difference, though'¦That's all his fault, boy, he don't know when to stop!' I agree!
Sonny then assumes the role of the stern taskmaster, devoting more than fifteen minutes to diligently work out the arrangement and subtle rhythmic nuances of the old standby, 'Friendly Galaxy.' First he tells Marshall Allen to play the melody on alto flute rather than piccolo, so the melody will 'cut through.' This seems counter-intuitive to me (the piccolo cuts through just fine) and indicative of his inexplicable ire towards Allen. Because then he starts to get angry and repeatedly reprimands Allen for playing 'on the beat!' Sun Ra scolds him: 'You been playing that number for ten years and can't play it yet!' Ra explains that he wants the melody played with 'anticipatory rhythms' ' a little bit ahead of the beat. 'If you play it right on time, you're gonna be wrong! It's designed for sound,' he says. Ra then demonstrates on the keyboard, playing the 'in-time' bassline and the 'out-of-time' melody simultaneously. 'See? I'm not asking you to do something I can't do. I'm doing it!' After a slightly more successful take, Sonny declares:
See, you almost played it that time because you wasn't counting and you wasn't thinking about it. You just have to do this like I'm talking. And I'm not measuring my words and saying, 'one-two-three''¦I can't do that. Music is a language, so you not supposed be counting. I might hold a word a little bit longer than usual if I want to emphasize what I'm saying. That's the way music is.
Ra goes on to talk about playing behind the beat and makes his point more explicit: 'That's hard to do too. So, it's either ahead or behind ' and then there's some music that's right on the beat. Well, white people can do that! When it's right on the beat, they got you!' After another run-through, Ra really starts to preach it:
It's all about togetherness. The white race is together. Don't let 'em fool you what they talking about revoltin' and revolutin'. What they got to revolute against? They got everything! But that's for you! ['¦] Talkin' about revolution. I told the truth the other night when I said, 'No. Not gonna have no revolution of black folks. Not no more freedom, not no peace, they don't need nothing like that. They need unity, precision, discipline.' That's it. That's the only thing white folks gonna respect and get out of the way ['¦] They got their stuff together and I got mine together. And I'm not afraid of them. I ain't worried about them. Now, I'm telling 'em that. It's about unity, precision, discipline ['¦] That's what jazz is: it's precision, discipline.
After some discussion, Ra calls for 'Intergalactic Universe,' a gently floating space vamp in 5/4 meter. The piece was never performed live and was likely never finished as you can hear Ra interrupting the proceedings several times in order to tweak the arrangement. Despite almost eighteen minutes of rehearsal, the music never quite gets off the ground although the piece clearly had some potential. Ra laments the lack of time for more rehearsal, but insists on working on another obscure composition, 'Living Myth 7,' a terrifically complicated melody in 7/4 which is through-composed in intricate, close harmony. The ensemble sounds tentative at best. After a lurching, half-time read-through, Ra calls for double-time but the Arkestra once more hobbles its way through the thorny score until the tape cuts off. Never played again, this is another tantalizing 'lost' work from Sun Ra's oeuvre.
Although none of the musical performances really hang together, this rehearsal fragment offers an intimate glimpse into Ra's working methods circa.1971 and his role as leader of the rag-tag Arkestra. At once genial storyteller, exacting schoolmarm, and political firebrand, Sonny clearly commanded attention and elicited a fierce loyalty from his most devoted disciples. As 'crazy' as Sun Ra might sound, he certainly got results. This tape recording allows a first-hand account of the fearsome charm by which Sun Ra achieved his ultimate aim: 'Unity, precision, discipline. That's it.'
Sam said...
About "Intergalactic Universe," you say: "a gently floating space vamp in 5/4 meter. The piece was never performed live." Actually, we now know that it was performed live at least 3 times! Here are the versions we have:

07. 1971-08? (15:13) from the ESP Radio Show. Same concert as "Universe in Blue," but in stereo. You mentioned this in your review of that LP: "a fifteen-minute 'Intergalactic Research' follows with another extended tenor workout from Gilmore." The mistake in the title is probably mine, although the Good Doctor May have announced it as such. This is a beautiful version, with a truly transcendent Gilmore solo. It ends with unaccompanied Gilmore.

08. Delft 1971-11-11 (18:42) This is another super-beautiful version, with Ra on piano. It's soulful, it swings, and it's got another killer Gilmore solo, and a wonderful Kwame Hadi trumpet outing. The vibes and flutes provide a nice two-chord background.

09. Mystery Board 1972-11-02 or -03 (9:09) Here's what I had to say about this, in the notes to "Live Highlights": "The only other place this composition is known to appear is on the rehearsal tapes before the European tour of 1971. [Again, we now know that's not the case!] That makes this a perfect example of the catalog of compositions band members have said they'd rehearse extensively before a show, only to never play it that night. Of course we don't have recordings of every single show from this tour, but it is interesting that it doesn't show up on even one. [Wrong again!] What amazes me is how Ra could neglect this wonderful piece; it certainly deserves more attention. It's a soul-jazz groove guided by Rocksichord/clavinet with the head beautifully executed by Gilmore, who then proceeds to play gorgeous variations. He just sounds fabulous. This solo is a gift. Anything that follows has to be anticlimactic, but Kwame Hadi's trumpet solo is compelling on its own terms--actually, it's quite beautiful! This is just a killer performance."
Rodger Coleman said...
Wow, Sam. You are amazing. You really should be doing this instead of me! I need to go back and listen to this again. I knew this sounded familiar on the Delft concert! Then there are all the unknown "Discipline" numbers....
Sam said...
Well, duh, I left off another performance of "Intergalactic Universe"--- 4. ca. 1972 (14:13) from "Intergalactic Research, The Lost Reel Collection vol. 2" (Transparency). There, it's mis-titled "Intergalactic Research." It's slightly slower than the other versions.

Upload Teddy Edwards Quartet, Amsterdam, August 1980

The Teddy Edwards Quartet at the International Jazz Festival Amsterdam (de Meervaart), Sunday 10 August, 1980. My own tape recording of the direct Dutch radio broadcast.

Jack Wilson has recorded with Dinah Washington and Gerald Wilson among others

Edwards, Jack Wilson, and Vinnegar were all three present at one Gerald Wilson session for Pacific Jazz in 1963. In March 1980, Jack Wilson played with the Clark Terry Five on Memories of Duke (Pablo), and in 1978 he recorded with Eddie Harris at the Keystone Korner in SF.

There are a two or three very short moments (c. 1 sec) of some audio distortion, which is in the original tapes (probably because of the direct live broadcasting). A very small part (fade out-fade in) is missing in the end of Serenade In Blue (tape flip).

Enjoy!

Last seeder's notes:
No conversion of any kind - this is the actual very hq broadcast signal!

It looks as if this is quite a discovery. I recorded this from Polish TV just the other day and it seems
that this is a virtually unknown Monk film shot in a Polish TV studio on Monk's first visit to Poland.

Kevin Foss on #dimeadozenjazzforum provided me with the following information:

Monk's fifth European tour (Spring 1966) took him into Poland for the first time. There was a 30 minute recording for Polish TV done sometime aroun April 4, 1966. There is a confirmed show in Warsaw that date, but there was also at least one other show in Poland (date and venue unknown) on that tour. There was also a BBC TV broadcast later that month, which has gone missing from the BBC vaults apparently.

The band for that tour was Monk/Rouse/Gales/Riley.

At the time of publication of Sheridan's discography on Monk (which to me is world's above any of the online discographies), there were no details on the Polish TV show. So this would be quite a find.

So here we go:

comments:
one of my early ventures, the 1st of 2 times I saw the Van Manakas trio and unfortunately I didn't get the whole show. Most of both sets are here, but a large chunk of the beginning is missing. I think we got to the show late because of a sellout but were able to get in when some left. what we did get on tape came out pretty well, no problems that I noticed in digitizing it. Couldn't find my 1st transfer so this is a new one, no CD
lineage in it for its 1st posting. If it was done with my deck, it was the 158, if my buddy's, a 156, not sure which we used this time. I thought this was a more energetic concert than the next one I saw (w/Barry Altschul replacing Bob Moses) but both were pretty nice. This one sounds a little like the Lester Bowie era Directions (without Lester) in parts, yet another of several
times I went to see someone and Vitous was the bassist. If you like Miroslav, Boston was a good place to be in late 70's. He played alot there at that time. Always sounded good too, here no exception. I have shared some of that and still
have a few others including one more with Manakas Altschul trio that is from October (and my master.) That will come in a few weeks, meanwhile one last Indy Day show for you that got left out of the last holiday torrent blitz. Manakas' guitar style doesn't really sound like anybody in particular, Maybe a little bit like Pat Martino/ Pat Metheny/ Ralph Towner, some of the mellower (not poppier) Benson, and I would say he is jazz. Pretty good jazz in this show. He does have at least one
studio release album (CD now), it's not heavy or light jazz, somewhere in between with a little bit of pop thrown in (not too much here).

Remastered in 2007 by grner1:
This was previously posted as a flawed unplayable DVD. Various rework methods were posted in the earlier seed comments but most of the programs used to do this probably involved re-encoding of the data. This version here did not involve any re-encoding of the media and better title and chapter menus were added. Since the original audio was LPCM, it could be extensively fine-tuned with Pro Tools - normalization of the very low levels by almost 15 dB, other level change repairs with silencing of blank spots, lots of clicks manually removed, plus some low end EQ boost to make the TV sound a bit less tinny-sounding. No digital noise reduction was used in the audio remastering process.

Here's the rest of the new lineage/remastering info:
The audio and video media was extracted losslessly by Cinematize 2 as elementary stream files. The video media is the same 2 files, though they were cropped tighter with DVD Studio Pro when authoring to clip the blank beginning and some of the l-o-o-o-n-n-g abc station ID that was at the end (cut to about 5 seconds from the original 30 seconds).

Show transcript details:
-- Opening credits 
-- Commercials: (1) Pruf spray starch; (2) Ultra-Brite toothpaste ad with couple flirting on airplane. (jingle: "Ultra-Brite gives your mouth...sex appeal"). 
-- Herb Alpert & the Tijuana Brass - "With A Little Help from My Friends" (instrumental) 
-- Herb Alpert (host) talks about his band, the Tijuana Brass, and their record company, A&M records. (All guests on this show recorded with A&M Records. The A in A&M Records was Herb Albert himself).
-- Liza Minnelli - "Happy Time" and "Mammy" 
-- Herb Alpert congratulates Liza on her recent marriage to Peter Allen. 
Commercial: Pepto-Bismol tablets 
-- Herb Albert introduces the Baja Marimba Band, who perform an instrumental song.

-- Wes Montgomery (jazz guitarist) - "Windy" (instrumental)

-- Herb notices a man sleeping in audience. He wonders what the man is dreaming about. This is followed by a dream sequence with Herb Alpert's instrumental songs: 
(1) "The Lonely Bull" (man dreams of being a bullfighter);

There are more chapter points than the selection menu indicates - every song, commercial and other interview/comedy bits not listed above can be accesse Separately while watching the DVD. 23 chapter points can be accessed from the selection menu but there are actually 49 selection points total. 

In the comments of the previous upload one person claimed that a lot of this show is lip-synched. I did not think so at first but after watching it a lot, now I'm not so sure. I can see at least one song where a guitar player has no guitar cord. The parts of the show that most interest Dime members - the Burt Bacharach, Wes Montgomery and Liza Minnelli songs are definitely NOT lip-synched, though possibly when Burt Bacharach is singing live, it May be the off-screen band's piano actually playing the piano part, not Burt. The Hollywood Palace had a large supplemental orchestra to back up the on-screen musicians, so just because the band members shown are not playing every part doesn't necessarily mean that it's all lip-synched. in any case, the the possibility of there being some lip-synched material has been cleared with the mods, so there should not be a risk of this being declared as violating Dime rules. And hopefully you will enjoy watching this DVD as much as I do!

+media.CE_lineage:
La Bussola was a famous venue in Versilia, a region just above the city of Viareggio, where lots of Italian and international stars performed over the years. Since Viareggio was the most popular town of the area, the venue was generally associated with it in spite being few kms north.
The famous concerts of La Bussola later moved few km south in a new venue called Bussoladomani (in Lido di Camaiore) where Miles Davis performed in 1990. Here is the 1st volume of a series of jazz shows that were broadcast by RAI tv.
Enjoy!

Various North Sea Jazz Fest - 1979-1981 - The Hague (The Netherlands)

Various artists
The Hague (North Sea Jazz Festival), the Netherlands
1979-1981

A combined c. 3-hr radio/TV broadcast for Dutch AVRO - AVRO's Jazz Night - o September 5/6 1981, with a selection from the NSJF years 1979-1981. From the recording on my reel-to-reel audio tape (I might also have the VHS videotape somewhere, but not sure). Announcements are by Pim Jacobs.

STOP AND READ THIS, IT'S IMPORTANT!

You know there are people out there who wouldn't like the idea that you are having so much fun listening to this music. They might, oh... want to regulate it, tax it, even take it away from you if they found out YOU were getting so much enjoyment out of something so simple. But you, oh you know better than that. This is YOUR private stash that your friends, your neighbors, even your mother shouldn't get hold of lest they corrupt it in some evil manner. Well meaning though they May be, no one must attempt to misguide you in your quest to get something as special as this - and to actually have fun playing it to death.

I shouldn't even be letting you in on it. But, there's something about your face that intrigues me. And yes, I heard this music twice yesterday and three times the day before that. You'll be doing the same thing.

Wardell Gray was one of the rising stars of post-war jazz, until his life was cut short at 34 under mysterious circumstances in Las Vegas. He would be much better known today had more recordings existed of him. He was a featured player with Earl Hines, Count Basie, and Benny Goodman and was a friend and frequent player with Dexter Gordon. His style was strong, powerful, and most importantly it was relaxed. This is not big-band music, but it does derive from it.

The early 1950's was a wonderful time for jazz, particularly if you lived in a big city. It was a time when you could walk into a small club and hear the likes of Miles Davis, Charlie Parker, Chet Baker, Dizzy Gillespie and others. In one respect it paralled the very early days of the modern rock movement, circa 1967. None of these people were stars to the extent that they are today and you could see them in small group settings in an intimate atmosphere. Although 52nd Street in New York was the epicenter of the small-group movement, you could find it in many other large cities.

This torrent consists of two completely different sets of circumstances, which somehow fit together perfectly. The first part is a radio broadcast fro April 28, 1951 at Birdland. It's of Count Basie's group in a small setting, featuring Mr. Gray blowing on the following tracks:

ledwhofloyd (Ross) notes:
This remaster uses from the audio files that glasnostrd19 previously balanced the levels of (which, in turn, came from mr_mags). This recording is fundamentally mono, so instead of trying to repair the the clipping on the left channel, I replaced it (monoized) with the unclipped right channel for those moments. I would guess I fully monoized about a third of the audio.

Before monoizing I phase aligned the channels, which required many different adjustments because it varied. On average the left was leading by around 6 samples. One of the reasons that the alignment of the channels kept changing is that there were a lot of slight discontinuities in the audio. While these discontinuities occurred throughout the audio, they were more heavily concentrated near the end. I would guess I repaired around 100 of them.

The original audio ran fast, and changed speed over the intermission. Speed adjusted in MATLAB.
Tracks 1-7: -2.5%
Tracks 8-20: -3.4%

There was a high frequency tracking signal around 16 kHz which was quite strong and audible, so I notch filtered it out. Except for the speed adjustment, I did all these edits in Audacity.

We're not 100% sure whether this is a soundboard or an FM. There are audience noises in the mix, so that suggests FM. At the very least it's not a pure soundboard. The tracking signal also suggests that it's FM. If it's FM sourced, than it might be possible that somebody made a better stereo capture of this show. As of 2022, this source from mr_mags is basically all that's been shared on dime. In 2010 alien156 shared a version from Herman which I don't have to directly compare, but based on the description provided I'm pretty sure it's from the same source as mr_mags' - just a different CD rip. If you think you have an upgrade, please consider sharing it.

This is an upgrade to torrent http://www.dimeadozen.org/torrents-details.php?id=748371
Better equalization which removes the boxiness and boominess typical for an audience recording.

I spent some hours applying the "harmonic balancing" approach using the Har-Bal software. The basic idea is to roughly match the spectrum of the recording to the spectrum of a good-sounding reference recording of the same music. Not slavishly, but with the small individual characteristics of the recording preserved, and always judging with your ears. The process is explained here:
http://auldworks.com/articles/audiorestorenew1.htm
(ignore the part about noise reduction

no noise reduction has been applied here). Of course, in the end it's nothing more than equalization, and a person with golden ears could do it with a multichannel equalizer.

The reference recording which I tried to approximate is of course "Footprints live", recorded the same year. To my ears, the result is spectacular. The boxy characteristic of an audience recording is gone

it now sounds like a professional on-stage recording. Check out the samples.
