CE_notes:
LDB Master Series #002

Hello, this is a collection of masters I would like to seed here. I've been taping shows for more than 25 years (in 2013 I will celebrate 30 years of happy recording hobby!) and have an awful lot of masters. These are in 
different formats, following the technological evolution: first on analogue cassettes, then MiniDisc, some DATs (I was borrowed a DAT machine to record some of the shows in late 90's / early 00's) and finally digital files
using Edirol R-09.

I've taped many shows of many artists over the years (both from audience and radio broadcasts) , so don't be surprised if you will find many different artists seeded! My music spectrum is quite wide, spanning from classical to hard rock.

Some shows are already circulating, some others have not circulated through collectors yet. But most of all, enjoy! They all come from my mastertapes!

Finally, some notes about your truly ldb: I have been a fan of live music since I was 9 years old (that is where I attended my very first show, a PFM/De André gig at Milano's Palalido) and my first taped show was at 11 using a crappy portable cassette player with embedded microphone. I become more serious about taping in 1983 when I started to record every show. In 1991 I acquired my first Sony Professional and in 2000 I moved to MiniDisc to finally settle on R-09 in early 2008.

I have seen nearly 500 shows in my career. Most of them were taped but for others bad luck struck and I could not record it: on top of my mind there's a Paul McCartney show in 1993 in Milano where I was caught by the security or Porcupine Tree in Roma in March 1999 when the DAT machine would seem to work but listening back to the tape there would just be a long bunch of silence. Or during a Y.Malmsteen show where I got so annoyed that I left halfway through the show and erased the tape and finally on a PFM show in Milano in 2007 where I had to leave before the encore because the baby-sitter had to leave early that evening. Some other times I was very close not to tape or had to do it in extremely difficult situations: for the four Peter Gabriel shows at Earls Court in 1987 security was checking tapers with metal detector

at the David Gilmour comeback show in London in 2001 at RFH I had the
security guy sitting next to me but I managed to tape the show without checking one single time my MiniDisc!

There was a time I was travelling anywhere in Europe to see shows, especially if there was no touring in Italy: I remember Rush in Paris in 1992 when the trio did not even know what Italy was. I have seen shows at stadiums (Genesis at Wembley) and in places with 30 people (Porcupine Tree in Milano in 1997)

bands that would later become huge (Pearl Jam in a free show for 150 people) and masters of jazz (Miles Davis or Sarah Vaughan). Shows I will never forget (Pink Floyd at Versailles castle) and some I would rather forget (no comment...).

I truly believe that live music is what keeps music alive, what make us enjoying it together, what allow us to have deep feelings and transmit it to others. Studio records are nowadays 'commodities': you can buy online as anonymous wav files and listen in your iPod or at home. Live music will always imply an effort to buy the tix, travel to the venue, see the show, think about it when coming back home.

I did not attend this particular show, but I was at the previous day's one in Villafranca, near Verona. This is possible the best jazz concert I've ever attended, at least in terms of piece of art. Four highly talented musicians, probably there are in the top 20 jazz musicians ever. What struck me during the performance was a mix of improvisation and perfect alignment among the musicians. I tend to label this band as a variation of Wayne's standard quartet with Patitucci and Perez replacing Herbie and Dave. It has the same kind of feeling and quite similar setlist. It was simply amazing. Perugia was their show at Umbria Jazz. This one comes from my master. Enjoy!

Before leaving to the New Morning for a spectacular Erik Truffaz show, I started the recording of the radio broadcast of a couple of Marciac shows. First, Shai Maestro, then the Wayne Shorter Quartet. Coming back home,
the show had just ended, so I took some time to edit it and seed it fresh from the oven!

Enjoy once more this french radio show from Wayne and let's celebrate him for his 80th birthday coming very soon!

Out of my 7,000+ shows and radio broadcasts, I have many concerts that were special for some reasons: the setlist, the musicians, the venue or unexpected events. These are the ones I'd like to propose you. Most of these come from my cassettes collection, so they will be released at a slower pace than my Master Series! But you won't be disappointed! I will try to gather the most unusual things I have in my collection and, as always, your feedback and comments will be my reward for all the work involved in this project.

Finally, some notes about your truly ldb: I have been a fan of live music since I was 9 years old (that is where I attended my very first show, a PFM/De André gig at Milano's Palalido) and my first taped show was at 11 using
a crappy portable cassette player with embedded microphone. I become more serious about taping in 1983 when I started to record every show. In 1991 I acquired my first Sony Professional and in 2000 I moved to MiniDisc to finally settle on R-09 in early 2008.

I have attended over 500 shows in my career. Most of them were taped but for others bad luck struck and I could not record it: on top of my mind there's a Paul McCartney show in 1993 in Milano where I was caught by the security or Porcupine Tree in Roma in March 1999 when the DAT machine would seem to work but listening back to the tape there would just be a long bunch of silence. Or during a Y.Malmsteen show where I got so annoyed that I left halfway through the show and erased the tape and finally on a PFM show in Milano in 2007 where I had to leave before the
encore because the baby-sitter had to leave early that evening. Some other times I was very close not to tape or had to do it in extremely difficult situations: for the four Peter Gabriel shows at Earls Court in 1987 security
was checking tapers with metal detector

at the David Gilmour comeback show in London in 2001 at RFH I had the security guy sitting next to me but I managed to tape the show without checking one single time my MiniDisc!

There was a time I was travelling anywhere in Europe to see shows, especially if there was no touring in Italy: I remember Rush in Paris in 1992 when the trio did not even know what Italy was. I have seen shows at stadiums (Genesis at Wembley) and in places with 30 people (Porcupine Tree in Milano in 1997)

bands that would later become huge (Pearl Jam in a free show for 150 people) and masters of jazz (Miles Davis or Sarah Vaughan). Shows I will never forget (Pink Floyd at Versailles castle) and some I would rather forget (no comment...).

I truly believe that live music is what keeps music alive, what make us enjoying it together, what allow us to have deep feelings and transmit it to others. Studio records are nowadays 'commodities': you can buy online as
anonymous wav files and listen in your iPod or at home. Live music will always imply an effort to buy the tix, travel to the venue, see the show, think about it when coming back home.

ldb

I've been reading the excellent Weather Report book, Elegant People by Curt Bianchi, lately. It's made me revisit recordings and shows I've loved for years which had been gathering a bit of dust. One thing that strikes me in their story is the constant personnel shifts around the Zawinul/Wayne axis, and how many drummers came and went until there was a bit more stability there through Peter Erskine and Omar Hakim. The book pointed out how much Zawinul loved Greg Errico, and how his arrival in the band really led them to solidify the direction shift that songs like Boogie Woogie Waltz and 125th St. Congress made. That of course signalled the beginning of the end of the Miroslav era and everything that led them to bigger audiences in the years that followed. It's clear from the book that Zawinul was really tough on the many great drummers that sat on WR's drum stool. That said, he seemed to love Errico, and it was apparently Errico's own decision to depart the band before ever heading into the studio (Mysterious Traveller would be next).
There have been some nice WR shares here lately, and there is one dating back to freeloader days in late 2021 from this band at Chateauvaillon in France. This particular show isn't active, and I'm not sure how long it's been off the tracker since I picked it up in 2013. Many thanks to whoever seeded it here back then, and to whoever recorded it back in the 70's.
Please support any of these musicians still with us by purchasing their officially released material, and by paying to see them live.

We are pleased to kick off a series of releases from a long time West Coast taper/collector that recently passed away. He transferred his extensive archives to CDR years prior to his passing and then passed it to a close friend. His friend has been involved in the West Coast music scene for the last five plus decades and understands the importance of getting these historic shows out to the collector's community. We are working closely reviewing the shows and researching current circulation as well as possible upgrades.

Our first release features Weather Report's opening set for Fleetwood Mac at the Sam Carver Gymnasium at Western Washington University in Bellingham, WA. This excellent quality capture took place during a transitional period for the band as they took on a more jazz-funk and groove oriented direction. You can hear the beginnings of this new direction they would explore even further into 1974 and beyond. Interestingly, this was a transitional period for Fleetwood Mac as well.

We've included newspaper ads, a pre and post review of the show. The reviewer of the show loved Weather Report and thought Fleetwood Mac was awful, the fact the gym had been recently rewired resulting in the gym's fans remaining off during the concert certainly did not help the mood. The review ends with Program Commissioner Nils Von Veh expressed hope that Weather Report would return to Western in the spring to perform in the Music Auditorium. Now that would be something.

Weather report did in fact return to Western on March 10th of the following year to perform in the auditorium, that show appears to have been previously shared but found to be lossy and banned. For those that may not have it, a lossless version from this newly acquired archive is in the not too distant future.

There are a number of folks we are indebted to for access to this exciting new archives, the anonymous West Coast collector, may he rest in peace, his friend that had the motivation and understands the need to get these historically important shows into circulation before they were lost forever and a huge thanks to dime member davmar77. He did not currently have the bandwidth to facilitate such an undertaking at this time and put us in touch...this is how dime should work.

Also, a big thanks to Goody, our pitch master, for not only getting this historically important show at the correct speed but going a step beyond by zeroing in on the setlist.

Dimers don't wait until it's too late to get those archives out into circulation.

If I'm reading the dimebot archive correctly, this show hasn't been up here before. I checked with a couple of people here too who I thought might know something, and it seemed new to them. This came to me in a trade and was simply marked "Weather Report-Chicago 1974". I'd assumed it was the show that's fairly well circulated from nearby Evanston later in 1974, but it isn't. According to the WR Annotated Discography gig page, the band did this gig at the Auditorium Theater in early July, so that is my guess for the time and place of what you'll be hearing in this show. If anyone knows diffently, please let us know in the comments.
You'll note that material from Mysterious Traveller is now sharing time in the setlist with things that had been in the live repertoire for a while. That album had been released in early Spring of 1974. Typical of WR, this is a great show. I know nothing about the circumstances of this recording, but it does sound like something that was professionally done. I matched the material played here and track times against any of the other 1974 shows I knew of, and this didn't seem to be a version of any of them. I'm happy if this is indeed new to any of us at this point, so many years after the event.Thanks to whoever traded this to me, and to whoever originally recorded this show and passed it on.
I'm moving this up a little in my seeding queue to mark the passing of the great Wayne Shorter. News of this just came across, so this is now here in tribute to him.

Here's another fine sounding WR show from 1974 that I had just about ready to go prior to learning of Wayne Shorter's passing (RIP). Unlike the shows I upped from Bellingham, WA and Chicago, this one had been up here before, but not since 2011. My copy came via a cd-r snail mail trade, so not exactly sure of the lineage, but I will share what was up here before when seeded by abbcccus or ricola.
This one does nod toward the current Mysterious Traveller album that came out a little over a half year before the gig. It's interesting for including a little of Wayne's Manolete from Sweetnighter married to Miroslav Vitous's final WR composition American Tango. Looking ahead, it also includes a slight nod towards Birdland which wouldn't take form for a few more albums.
Thanks to the trader who made this available to me, and to whoever recorded it and distributed it from then to now. Once again, upped now in tribute to Wayne in keeping a big part of his musical legacy alive.

Here's another WR show I'm upping to honor the life and legacy of Wayne Shorter. I shared a few shows recently from 1974 WR, and I'll now up a few more from 1975. Guessing that many more people are familiar with the peak of their popularity in the late 70's and their association then with Jaco Pastorius, so I'm hopeful that some folks might gain an appreciation of other WR incarnations while we mourn and celebrate Wayne. 
In most ways of looking at the band, 1974 and 1975 were the post Miroslav and pre-Jaco years. That was the time when I first saw them and got into them through Mysterious Traveller and going to a few shows. To me, these were the Alphonso years. I play bass, and have always loved Alphonso Johnson and what he brought to the band at this time. He particularly seemed to come into his own on these '75 shows, and although my jaw might've dropped open a bit wider when first seeing Jaco with the band, my jaw (and ears) had already been opened wide many times via Alphonso and how he grooved so inventively. He was grooving in the rhythm section at this point with percussionist Alyrio Lima and drummer Chester Thompson (post Zappa and pre Genesis). At the point of this show, they were touring the Tale Spinnin' album that had come out in May, 1975 and 3 of the songs here came from that recording. Wayne wrote Freezing Fire. According to the WR Annotated Discography gig page, the date here is now regarded as being correct.
All in all, the band was was a great vehicle for all of the musicians involved over the time of WR's run, and all credit had to go to the "big names" that initially and consistently caused people to pay attention, Joe Z and Wayne. Those 2 provided much of the framework through their compositions and guidance, although the bassists did chip in too with some great compositions or co-compositions. Thanks to the trader who'd made this available to me, and to whoever first recorded and distributed this. My copy came to me in a cd-r snail mail trade, but this was last up on DIME in 2011 when it was shared by michaelmee, and was here as early as 2005 from jazzcdburner. This was shared then as either a SBD or FM.

Welcome to Volume 57 of our master series featuring the master recordings of dime member "tapetyrant". The series will predominately feature captures in the Northeast and Southern California areas. We will touch on multiple genres with a strong focus on Jazz Fusion, New Wave and Rock.

Tapetyrant was an active taper in the 1980's and much of the 1990's before, like many of us, hanging up the mics. What he captured during that time is uniformly excellent quality and his master tapes have been safely stored, the first batch are in pristine condition. Some shows may circulate from lower generation copies but most have remained uncirculated until now and have never circulated directly from the masters.

Prior to DAT, the heavy lifting was entirely done by a Sony D5 with NAK 300's and taping was serious business, acquiring the best seats possible and working to keep neighbors in check.

For Volume 57 we return to one TapeTyrant's top 3 bands with a stunning capture of Weather Report's 1983 Beacon Theatre show. Once again we are gifted with another show that appears to be previously unheard from Tyrant's amazing master archives.

Thanks as always to Goody for the continued pitch guidance and filling in a gap in the setlist.

Continued thanks to "tapetyrant" for doing such a great job capturing these historic shows, for reaching out and entrusting me to present his excellent work for all to enjoy for decades to come. We are indebted to his generosity (tapers don't let those tapes and your hard work get lost to the ages, there are plenty of folks to get in touch with here to help get them out, we're all working to leave no tape behind).

"Christmas Jazz for Kids"
Alfried Krupp Saal/Philharmonie, Essen (Germany)
December 22, 2005 - remastered RESEED

This matinee concert (in which I was positioned at the back of the hall, so the sound is somewhat distant) took place in front of an audience including at least 500 children, aged about 10-12, and this can be heard clearly in the audience reactions. The Kollektief sometimes presents special programs for children, in which they accentuate their theatre-like approach.
Because of the time of year, at some point, the Kollektief played "O Tannenbaum", giving Andy Altenfelder the opportunity to conduct the audience. As usual, during "Morribreuk" Andy Altenfelder and Boy Raaymakers entered the concert hall from the sides, decending the stairs whilst playing until hugging each other on stage, blowing into the other member's trumpet. During "Heibel", Willem appeared dressed in a monkey's costume, and took over control of the piano. He then invited some of the kids to play together with him.
Afterwards, still dressed up this way, he played some solo parts on sax. 
During "Acros", Boy is being sawn in half, and during "The Bottles", the "bottle-phone" is played.

Seeding this to mark the passing of Mick Goodrick. He is one of those guys probably known most as a teacher and "guitarit's guitarist. He was a longtime resident of the Boston area and he had a lot to do with teaching there at Berklee. His association on 1970's ECM albums saw him teamed with a younger up and coming player named Pat Metheny in Gary Burton's group. He was also associated with John Abercrombie, John Scofield, Bill Frisell, and Wolfgang Muthspiel, as he is here. He didn't record or tour as prolifically as any of these other player, but he was revered by all of them, and many younger players who followed in their wake.
The only time I saw him perform was when he was a member of Jack DeJohnette's Special Edition during the late 80's when they recorded a couple of albums for Impulse. His only leader dates were one album for ECM in the mid 70's, and another for CMP called Biorhythms in about 1990. He recorded with Muthspiel in a trio along with Dave Liebman on CMP, and then in a duo for a live album they recorded and released on Muthspiel's Material Records label from 2008.
I'm sure that this came to me in a cd-r snail mail trade. I'm not sure if it's been on DIME (I couldn't find it in the dimebot archive). Thanks to whoever recorded it and whoever made it available to me. That said, it's tough to figure this all out. The songs were tracked haphazardly, and that meant the end of one track often contained empty space followed by nearly 10 seconds of the following track. That meant the following track would begin in progress. I've re-tracked this all now in Audacity so that these issues are no longer a factor. It's also weird in that any applause or between song banter has been edited out, except towards the end of the performance where Goodrick introduces himself and his composition to be played next. You'll hear him say most of the music was written by Muthspiel. Regrettably, there's nothing to identify the bassist or drummer.
RIP, Mick Goodrick, and here's hoping that a few more shows that included him might be shared now in tribute. A few things are running already that include him, but not this particular show.

Recently found deep in my archives, I don't think this has been on DIME before. My favorite version of the Zawinul Syndicate is with Scott Henderson (Tribal Tech) on guitar. This is a decent soundboard capture from the 1988 European tour, alhough a little hissy on the quiet sections. The soundman makes a lot of volume adjustments/boosts to various instruments throughout so levels do
fluctuate here and there, but nothing that detracts from this high energy show. I've attempted to compensate for the uneven volume adjustments using Adobe Audition. Even though the crowd is very distant and quiet, this show still rocks.

2022 Info- I'm happy to currently be picking up some Wayne Shorter shows I hadn't gotten before in a bit of a flood happening now (thank for that!). Wayne invariably gets me thinking of Joe. I took a look at what's currently up here from the Syndicate, and surprisingly, nothing seems to have been upped from them in about a year. I then took a look to see what I had that I could easily seed or re-seed, given that it was recently Joe Z's posthumous birthday, and this is an active festival season in Europe during which the Syndicate was often active.
That led me to this show, which took place 27 years ago today. This was a typically hot version of the Syndicate with top notch band members. It's definitely not everything that would've been performed, but it's very interesting because it shows Joe Z and the Syndicate calling John McLaughlin and the Free Spirits up to the stage for a run through of Weather Report's Corner Pocket. Paco Sery and Dennis Chambers together? Apparently, so. Joey De Francesco doesn't duel it out with Joe Z on keys, but shows his ample skills on trumpet here. Of course, there's the one and only (and currently active on this year's Festival circuit), John McLaughlin- hoping to see some shares of those 2022 sets here.
I got this as a DIME share here at least 5 years ago, so big thanks to whoever upped it then, and to whoever had recorded it and circulated it in the first place. You'll see in the copy of the info below that this was seeded then as being "possibly new to circulation" at that time. No samples here, as referenced in the earlier info. Sorry.

This is a fairly uncirculated Syndicate show, which I'm re-seeding after upping it here several years ago. It's a liberated boot that I actually bought in a used record store in Greenwich Village in NYC not too long after the show was performed. Joe and the Syndicate were in between the My People, World Tour and Faces and Places albums. Joe actually wrote and recorded Mauthausen at this point, his recollection of growing up in Austria during WW2 and under Nazi rule.
This document of the Syndicate in Georgia is a particularly good show for me in that it features a Syndicate that included the late, great Victor Bailey (the man who replaced Jaco in WR) on bass. Here, he actually is featured on his own Do You Know/Continuum, that was one of the finest tributes to Jaco that I know of. That was on Victor's 1999 album called Low Blow.
Not sure exactly where/how the music on this disc was recorded, but it's definitely a professional recording that May have been either a soundboard, or a local (Georgian) FM or video broadcast. Thanks to whoever May have recorded this, and circulated it to the point that I found it in NYC.

Here's another Joe Z and Syndicate show that I had easily accessible for this re-seed. Like the 1995 show, this is from Festival Season at the North Sea Jazz Festival. Here we find an ailing Joe during his final run with the Syndicate. He passed away in September of 2007. There's a poignant moment in the excellent Weather Report book, Elegant People, where Joe meets up one final time with Wayne Shorter in Austria. Wayne was on tour with his band, and Joe was not long for this world. He was still at it, though, and always up for the music, as he is here. This set finds the Syndicate doing a pretty even mix of songs from their own output along with some Weather Report songs. Hot stuff from a hot band.
Thanks to the seeder that upped this when I grabbed it, and to whoever recorded it an circulated the show. CD covers were included by the seeder I got this from. I've included them here, and thanks to whoever created them.
